MN202611_q79ga7chal.t:
Kevin Gautier Kayisire (L) and Crépin Gontran Kayisire (R)

Many small businesses in Rwanda, and across Africa still rely on handwritten records to track sales, manage stock and monitor their finances.

You will find them keeping pens and notebooks, in what is called pen-and-paper records.

A Rwandan startup, founded by brothers Crepin and Kevin Kayisire, is seeking to change that through a digital platform that brings these functions together and gives business owners a clearer picture of how their enterprises are performing.

Crepin and Kevin Kayisire, graduates of the African Leadership University (ALU), founded Kayko in 2021. The company provides software that helps small businesses move away from handwritten records and manage their daily operations digitally.

The idea emerged from a problem they had seen among small businesses in their communities. Many shop owners, salon operators and other small enterprises relied on pen-and-paper records or software that was not designed for the realities of informal businesses across Africa.

The brothers sought to develop a simpler solution. Their platform allows businesses to record sales, manage inventory, track expenses and maintain financial records. It also provides real-time information that owners can use to understand their business performance and make decisions.

The project began as a final-year capstone project at ALU. The university’s emphasis on practical learning, leadership and problem-solving helped shape the idea.

Crepin Kayisire has been previously quoted saying the university’s first-year Leadership Core programme helped him understand how to identify problems and develop solutions.

Company CEO Crepin Kayisire speaking at Africa Week 2025 at Norrsken House Kigali

He said the programme exposed students to leadership, communication, data-driven decision-making, project management and the identification of global challenges and opportunities.

These skills helped him conceptualise the business idea that later became Kayko.

The platform’s impact is reflected in the experience of some of its users.

Gisele Irasubiza, a shop owner in Busanza, Kigali, previously struggled to manage her inventory and understand the financial position of her business.

Kayko enabled her to monitor different aspects of the business remotely. She can now access the information whether she is at her shop, at another job or away from the premises.

The company has since expanded beyond its original bookkeeping services. It now reports serving more than 15,000 businesses across seven African countries.

In December 2025, Kayko raised $1.2 million from investors, including Burrow Capital, Luxembourg Development Agency, Hanga Ignite and develoPPP Ventures.

The funding is intended to support the expansion of its platform and the development of lending services. The company plans to use financial records generated by businesses on its system to assess their needs and offer working-capital financing.

The founders are also preparing to introduce card payments through mobile phones. This would allow merchants to accept card payments alongside the platform’s existing business management services.

Kayko recently completed a Payment Card Industry Data Security Standard (PCI DSS) assessment, validated on November 10, 2026, by Digital Jewels Africa.

The assessment addresses the protection of cardholder data. However, it does not by itself authorise the company to provide regulated payment services in Rwanda. It must also meet the relevant requirements set by the National Bank of Rwanda.

The proposed service would place Kayko in competition with established merchant payment providers such as Flutterwave, Paystack and Pesapal. Its approach combines payment services with bookkeeping, inventory management and access to financing.

The expansion comes as Rwanda’s payment market remains heavily dominated by mobile money, while card transactions account for a much smaller share.

Kevin Kayisire speaking at function in Kigali

According to the National Bank of Rwanda, mobile merchant transactions increased by 40 per cent to 588 million in the year ended June 2025. Card transactions declined by 23 per cent to 1.6 million over the same period.

However, the value of card transactions increased by 18 per cent to Rwf157 billion.

The Central Bank’s October 2026 report placed point-of-sale payments at approximately 1 per cent of GDP, compared with 174 per cent for mobile payments.

These figures show the challenge facing companies seeking to expand card acceptance. They also point to room for growth as businesses adopt more digital payment and financial management tools.

Kayko’s plans go beyond helping merchants record transactions. By using business data to assess financial performance, the company wants to help small enterprises access loans that might otherwise be difficult to obtain.

The founders have previously emphasised the importance of building a reliable service in Rwanda before expanding further into other markets.

Their ambition is to make financial management easier for small businesses while giving them tools to grow, access financing and participate more fully in the digital economy.

Bonnie Tyler died aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year

Bonnie Tyler sings of "love, light and peace" and remembers "the ones who still live on inside our hearts" on her posthumous Christmas single, which was released on Friday.

The popular Welsh powerhouse singer, born Gaynor Hopkins, died in July aged 75 after undergoing emergency intestinal surgery in Portugal earlier this year.

Fans were able to hear the Total Eclipse of the Heart singer's husky tones one more time on the festive track titled "Love, Light and Peace".

The last song Tyler recorded features sleigh bells and angels and an ad-libbed farewell: "To all, goodnight."

The lyrics about grief and loss take on new meaning following her death.

Tyler sings: "Blessed are the ones who still live on inside our hearts.

The song was written by Chrissie Hammond and Grammy-winner Terry Britten, who played guitar on Tyler's debut album, The World Starts Tonight in 1977.

Nearly 50 years later, he returned as a writer and producer for the last song she recorded.

Tyler had "no big ideas" about recording until she was spotted by a talent scout

Tyler's husband of more than 50 years, Robert Sullivan, previously said she would have wanted fans to hear the music she was working on, and gave his blessing for the song's release .

Tyler was born in a Neath council house where she grew up with a love of music before being discovered by talent scout Roger Bell in a Swansea club.

After finding fame she was dubbed "the female Rod Stewart" for her husky vocals, and launched a career that spanned 50 years .

In August, fans travelled to Swansea to line the streets as a celebration of life service was held for her at Swansea Minster.

Foreign Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe with incumbent Francophonie Secretary-General Louise Mushikiwabo at the Ministerial Session this Saturday

The Democratic Republic of Congo (DRC) has withdrawn its candidate from the race for Secretary-General of the International Organisation of La Francophonie (OIF), but its decision to support a Romanian contender instead of another African candidate has drawn criticism from Rwanda.

In a statement issued on November 14, following the 48th Francophonie Ministerial Conference in Phnom Penh, Cambodia, the Congolese government announced the withdrawal of Juliana Amato Lumumba, saying the move was intended to encourage consensus among member states.

Kinshasa said it wanted to help overcome divisions that had emerged during the selection process and preserve unity within the organisation. It also praised Lumumba’s commitment and qualifications, saying her withdrawal should not be interpreted as a reflection on her abilities.

However, the DRC announced that it would now support Romanian candidate Dacian Cioloș, following consultations with Romania. The two countries said their joint position was aimed at bringing member states together around a common candidate.

Reacting to the announcement, Rwanda’s Foreign Affairs Minister Olivier Nduhungirehe welcomed Lumumba’s withdrawal, saying it could help build consensus around Rwanda’s candidate, Louise Mushikiwabo, who is seeking another term as Secretary-General.

In a statement posted on X, Nduhungirehe said the withdrawal also weakened arguments that the Francophonie risked becoming caught in a political confrontation between Rwanda and the DRC through their respective candidates.

However, the minister questioned why Kinshasa had chosen to support a Romanian candidate rather than one of the remaining African contenders.

He said the decision went against an African Union resolution adopted in Addis Ababa on July 28–29, 2026, which endorsed three African candidates for the Francophonie leadership position.

The resolution, EX.CL/Dec.1361(XLIX), called on the 27 African countries that are members of the Francophonie to agree on one of the three candidates, with the aim of keeping the organisation’s top position in African hands.

The three African candidates endorsed by the AU were Mushikiwabo, Lumumba and Mauritania’s Coumba Bâ.

With Lumumba now out of the race, Nduhungirehe argued that the DRC’s decision to back Cioloș rather than either of the two remaining African candidates undermines the collective position adopted by African governments.

He called on African Union member states, under the chairmanship of Burundi, to take note of the development.

The Francophonie leadership contest has attracted particular attention because it involves both Africa’s representation in international institutions and diplomatic relations between Rwanda and the DRC.

KIGALI – When a premature baby or a newborn who experienced complications survives and is discharged from hospital, for most families, the struggle does not end there.

At home, parents must support the child’s development, while often navigating the need for specialized services, uncertainty about the child’s future, and the added burden of stigma and social isolation.

For families raising children with developmental disabilities, everyday activities such as feeding, communication and movement may require patience, practical knowledge and continued support.

Yet many parents leave hospital without a clear understanding of what to expect as their children grow, where to seek help or how to respond when developmental milestones are delayed.

For Angelique Murekatete, a 39-year-old mother of four, the journey began on July 10, 2025, when she gave birth prematurely to a baby girl at Nyarugenge hospital.

Although her daughter received the necessary medical care despite the difficulties surrounding her early arrival, bringing her home was only the beginning of another demanding journey.

“There were times when I worried whether my daughter would grow like other children. You want to see your child reach the expected milestones, but when progress is slow, you sometimes wonder what lies ahead,” she says.

The uncertainty has not taken away her hope. She draws encouragement from the steady progress her daughter continues to make, believing that with patience, time and appropriate care, she will grow into a healthy and strong person.

“I have learned to appreciate every little improvement. She may not be developing at the pace I expected, but I believe she will continue growing. As a mother, I cannot give up on her,” she says.

Her experience reflects a challenge facing Rwanda’s health system as more premature and medically vulnerable newborns survive.

Keeping babies alive is a critical achievement, but ensuring they receive appropriate developmental support after leaving hospital remains an equally important responsibility.

A Rwandan program designed to address some of these gaps provides evidence that structured follow-up and family support can improve the lives of children at risk of developmental disabilities and their caregivers.

The Pediatric Development Clinic (PDC)-Baby Ubuntu model, developed by the Ministry of Health in partnership with Partners in Health (PIH) and other stakeholders, combines clinical follow-up for high-risk infants with practical group sessions for caregivers.

Its effectiveness was assessed in a cluster randomized trial involving 1,247 children across 56 health centers in Burera, Kamonyi and Gakenke districts.

Of these, 567 had developmental disabilities. The study is described in a policy brief as the largest trial of an early childhood intervention for children at risk of developmental disability in sub-Saharan Africa.

Dr, Erick Baganizi, Head of Division for Clinical Programs at PIH.

Among families caring for children with developmental disabilities, 66.1 per cent in the intervention group recorded a meaningful improvement in quality of life, compared with 42.9 per cent in the comparison group.

Caregiver psychological distress also fell, with 27 per cent of caregivers in the intervention group experiencing distress, against 42.8 per cent in the comparison group. The study further recorded improvements in caregiver confidence and reduced disability-related stigma.

One caregiver described how she had previously avoided taking her child outside because people mocked the family and called the child a “monster”. After participating in the sessions, she began taking the child everywhere and educating others, who gradually became more accepting.

Dr, Erick Baganizi, Head of Division for Clinical Programs at PIH says that this attention to caregivers is central to the program.

“We tend to take care of the child, but we forget about the family. If you forget the family, where the child goes back after discharge from the hospital, then you are not doing a good job for the caregiver,” he noted.

Stakeholders during during discussions about The Pediatric Development Clinic (PDC)-Baby Ubuntu model at a recent gathering in Kigali.

The trial also found that hospitalization among children with developmental disabilities was lower in the intervention group, at 13.7 per cent, compared with 22.4 per cent in the comparison group.

However, there was no measurable improvement in child development, functional status or growth at the end line assessment, conducted only three weeks after the intervention ended. Longer-term follow-up will be necessary to establish whether the program produces changes in these outcomes.

The model has since been integrated into 82 health centers and seven hospitals across five districts. All 29 health centers involved in the trial’s intervention arm were still delivering it a year later.

Preliminary costing puts the average first-year expense at about $280 per child, falling to approximately $153 annually once the program is fully established.

About 90 per cent of recurrent costs relate to nurses’ time and health-center space already provided by government, although expansion will require investment in training, mentorship and service capacity.

The Permanent Secretary in the Ministry of Health Jean Marie Vianney Ndayizigiye said Rwanda’s ambition must extend beyond ensuring newborn survival.

“Our ambition must go beyond ensuring that children survive. We must ensure that each and every child has the opportunity to grow and reach their full potential,” he said.

Policy recommendations call for the model to become a national standard for following up high-risk newborns, with phased expansion to health centers in every district. They also propose integrating relevant training into nursing curricula and establishing sustainable financing.

For mothers like Angelique, however, the importance of such support is measured in the everyday progress of their children. Her daughter’s journey may be slower than she initially expected, but she remains hopeful about what lies ahead.

Ultimately, saving a premature baby’s life is only the first step. Ensuring that the child continues to receive the care and support needed to grow and reach their potential is the responsibility that follows.

Repubulika Iharanira Demokarasi ya Congo (RDC) iri gutanga urugero rukomeye rw’ibi. Mu gihe i Kinshasa hagaragazwa inyota yo kugira uruhare rukomeye mu miyoborere y’Umuryango w’Ibihugu bikoresha Igifaransa (OIF), ibigo by’Abanyekongo byagize uruhare mu gutegura Imikino ya Cyenda ya Francophonie biracyategereje kwishyurwa, kandi hashize imyaka irenga itatu imikino ibaye.

Amakuru yatangajwe n’ibyo bigo byishyize hamwe mu ihuriro ry’ubucuruzi, avuga ko bitarishyurwa imirimo byakoze ijyanye no kubaka no kuvugurura ibikorwaremezo byakoreshejwe muri iyo mikino.

Ikindi gihangayikishije kurushaho, ni uko bivuga ko nubwo inyandiko zemeza ko amafaranga agomba kwishyurwa zashyizweho umukono mu buryo bw’ikoranabuhanga, ayo mafaranga ataragera kuri konti zabyo za banki.

Nyamara ibyo bigo byari byitabiriye ubusabe bwa Leta ya Congo mu kazi kihutirwa. Byakoresheje abakozi babyo, ibikoresho n’amafaranga yabyo kugira ngo bifashe Kinshasa kubahiriza ibyo yari yarijeje no kwereka amahanga ko ishobora gutegura neza igikorwa mpuzamahanga.

Ubu, ibigo byagize uruhare mu gutuma igihugu cyigaragaza neza ku rwego mpuzamahanga ni byo byirirwa bisaba Leta yabihaye akazi kubishyura ibyo ibabereyemo.

Mbega gushimirwa! Mbega kubahiriza inshingano!

Ibi birushaho kugaragaza ikibazo gikomeye, cyane ko Guverinoma ya Congo isa n’aho ihugiye cyane mu nyota yo kugira ijambo mu bya dipolomasi no mu nzego mpuzamahanga, aho kwita ku kubahiriza inshingano zayo z’amafaranga ifitiye ibigo by’abikorera bo mu gihugu cyayo.

Ni gute Guverinoma igorwa no kwishyura amadeni yayo yakwishyira imbere nk’ishobora kuyobora umuryango mpuzamahanga wose?

Kuyobora OIF ntibivuze gusa kugaragaza inyota ya politiki, kuvuga amagambo menshi mu nama za dipolomasi cyangwa gushaka kugira ijambo rikomeye mu bihugu bikoresha Igifaransa. Bisaba no kugaragaza umuco wo kubazwa inshingano, gukorera mu mucyo, imiyoborere myiza no kubahiriza ibyo umuntu yiyemeje.

OIF si igihembo cya dipolomasi igihugu cyifuza gutwara mu gihe ibigo byacyo bwite byatereranywe, bikaba biri mu bibazo by’amafaranga.

Ikibazo gihangayikishije kurushaho ni ingaruka ibi bigira ku bigo birebwa n’iki kibazo. Inyuma y’ayo mafaranga atarishyurwa hari abakozi, abagemurira ibyo bigo ibikoresho, imiryango, ishoramari n’ibikorwa by’ubukungu byahungabanyijwe no kutubahiriza amasezerano ya Leta.

Gusaba ibigo gukora imirimo mu gihe gito cyane, gukoresha umutungo wabyo mu gutegura igikorwa mpuzamahanga, hanyuma bikamara imyaka myinshi bitarishyurwa, ni ikibazo gikomeye giteye inkeke.

Iryo huriro ry’ibigo risigaye risaba Minisitiri w’Imari gutangaza ingengabihe isobanutse igaragaza igihe azishyurira imyenda Leta ibifitiye. Ni ubusabe bw’ibanze budakwiye no kuba ngombwa ko ibyo bigo bishyira hamwe ngo bibusabe, nyuma y’imyaka myinshi bitegereje kwishyurwa.

Mbere yo kwifuza kuyobora OIF, Kinshasa ikwiye kubanza kubahiriza inshingano zayo imbere y’Abanyekongo.

Kuko ubuyobozi ntibugaragarizwa mu magambo avugirwa mu nama za dipolomasi, ahubwo bugaragazwa n’ibikorwa. Iyo igihugu gisaba umwanya ukomeye ku rwego mpuzamahanga, ariko ibigo byacyo bwite bikaba birirwa bigikurikirana ngo kibishyure, ikibazo ntikiba kikiri ku nyota yacyo yo kugira ijambo gusa, ahubwo n’icyizere kigirirwa n’abandi kiba kiri mu kaga gakomeye.

Stargazers are being treated to a diagonal parade of four planets in the pre-dawn sky throughout November.

Mercury, Venus, Mars and Jupiter will all be visible to the naked eye in the south-eastern to eastern sky.

Particularly notable will be the line-up on Monday 16 November when Mars and Jupiter will appear exceptionally close together, according to the Royal Museums Greenwich.

From 24 November, a full Moon - the first of a run of four supermoons - will also join the planets in the morning sky.

Mercury will be the hardest planet to spot in the parade.

As the closest planet to the Sun and the smallest in our solar system, it is permanently locked in solar glare.

It is only visible in twilight and never in a fully dark sky. As always it will be dim and close to the horizon.

Try spotting it in a wide open sky with a flat horizon and look to the south-east.

Venus shines in the night sky above a waxing crescent Moon

Above Mercury and toward the right, you will spot Venus.

Venus is an easy planet to find as it is the brightest object in our night sky after the Moon. It has the highest albedo of any major planet in our solar system - that is reflects more sunlight back into space thus appearing brighter.

It is also usually the closest planet to Earth in its orbit - a mere 24 million miles away at times. It is a similar size too.

It will be higher in the sky than Mercury and visible earlier in the night in the hours before sunrise.

Don't mistake it with the bright star Spica which will be close to it. Stars twinkle while planets glow steadily.

Mars and Jupiter will appear to be very close to each other in the sky on the 15 and 16 November.

Mars is currently high in the eastern sky, with Jupiter below but appearing brighter.

"They will be separated by just 1.2 degrees, or roughly the width of a finger held at arm's length," according to Gideon Bendavid-Walker, astronomer at the Royal Observatory Greenwich.

The two planets will appear close to the bright star Regulus and may even look like a triple star.

If you have binoculars or a telescope then a few other bonus planets will also be visible this month.

At a similar time before sunrise, Uranus will be setting in the west. Then Saturn and Neptune will also be visible for a time in the evening rather than the morning sky.

Pre-dawn on Monday could bring better viewing conditions for more of the UK

Sunday night is forecast to be drier, as the day's rain and hill snow clear. However, wintry showers will pester northern Scotland with plenty of cloud.

Also the odd shower will pop up around north-west facing coasts.

Otherwise, the night looks mostly clear and dry, apart from the odd mist of fog patch.

To view the parade, find a spot away from light pollution with a good view of the eastern horizon and let your eyes adjust to the dark for around twenty minutes.

The best time to view the planetary lineup is approximately 45-60 minutes before sunrise.

Perezida Vladimir Putin w'Uburusiya avuga ko yipfuriza Ukraine "amahoro arama".

Ariko ni na we yagomoreye ingabo ziwe kuri ico gihugu kibanyi mu ntambara yeruye imaze imyaka hafi itanu, kandi akabandanya yanka iciyumviro c'uguhagarika intambara burundu.

None kuri Moscou (ubutegetsi bw'Uburusiya), ni igiki gikenewe kugira habe amahoro?

Kremlin (ibiro vy'umukuru w'igihugu c'Uburusiya) yarabitomoye inyuma y'ibiganiro yagiranye n'intumwa za Amerika Steve Witkoff na Jared Kushner: "Uburyo bushasha bw'igihe kirekire bwo gucungera umutekano n'amahoro ata nkunzi."

Mu mvugo yoroshe, ibi bisigura ko Moscou ishaka guhindura intunganyo y'umutekano wa Buyara ku buryo yoba akunguko ku Burusiya.

Ivyo Uburusiya buriko burasaba bishobora kuvamwo impinduka za mbere zikomeye cane mu bijanye n'umutekano w'Uburaya kuva intambara y'ukwikekana (guerre froide/Cold War) irangiye.

Kremlin yongeye gushira imbere icipfuzo cabwo co muri Kigarama (12) 2021 casaba OTAN (urunani rwo kwivunira umwansi hamwe ruhurikiyemwo ibihugu vy'Uburengero) kutabandanya yiyagurira akarere yerekeza mu buseruko, be no gutanga ivyemezo ko ibihugu nka Ukraine na Géorgie bitazokwigera vyemererwa kuyinjiramwo.

Uburusiya kandi bwasavye ko OTAN igabanya canke ikura ibikorwa vyayo vya gisirikare mu bihugu vy'Uburaya bwo Hagati n'Ubuseruko vyinjiye muri uru runani inyuma y'irasambuka ry'Ubumwe bw'Abasoviyeti.

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Abakuru b'ibihugu vy'Uburengero ico gihe bamiriye kure ivyo vyifuzo, bavuga ko ari nk'itegeko Uburusiya bwashatse kubahatirako. Inyuma y'amezi abiri, bwaciye butanguza igitero cabwo gikomeye kuri Ukraine.

Ivyo vyipfuzo vyari vyarashizwe ku ruhande. Ariko Kremlin yongeye kubigarukana muri ibi biganiro vya poritike mpuzamakungu.

Ikindi kandi, Yuri Ushakov, umwe mu bajenama ba Putin mu bijanye n'imigenderanire, yavuze ko Moscou iri mu kwongerako "ibindi vyipfuzo bishasha" ku rutonde rw'ivyo isaba, ifatiye ku co ifata ko ari amayeri y'Uburengero yo kurondera "gutsinda Uburusiya".

Gusa ibi si ukuvuga ko ibihugu vy'Uburengero bizovyemera.

Ariko kuba ikibazo c'umutekano w'Uburayi ubu kiriko kiravugirwa mu biganiro vyerekeye Ukraine, bifatwa nk'intsinzi ya Moscou.

Mu ntango z'ino ndwi, ikinyamakuru Komsomolskaya Pravda canditse kiti: "Muri Kigarama 2021, Uburusiya bwarasavye ku mugaragaro ko OTAN isubira kwihweza intunganyo yayo i Buraya.

"Mu gihe rero ubu tumaze gutsinda urugamba rumwe mu guhatira Uburengero gutangura kwiyumvira ikibazo c'umutekano, abantu bacu bajejwe imigenderanire bakeneye gutsinda urundi mu gutuma Uburengero bufata nka nkama impungenge z'Uburusiya zijanye n'uko OTAN ibandanya yiyagurira akarere."

Ayandi makuru yacu mushobora kuyakurikira kuri YouTube kuri BBC News Gahuza

Kaja Kallas ajewe imigenderanire mu muryango w'Ubumwe bwa Buraya avuga ko ivyo Uburusiya busaba bijanye n'intunganyo nshasha y'umutekano wa Buraya ari "umutego" ufise intego yo "gusamaza kugira ntihabe amasezerano yo guhagarika intambara".

Yanditse ku mbuga nyagiro ati: "Intunganyo y'ibiganiro hagati ya Ukraine n'Uburusiya ni ikintu gihambaye. Ico gushira imbere kuruta ibindi ni ukubanza gushika ku masezerano yo guhagarika intambara, hagaca hakurikira amasezerano y'amahoro. Ico gihe ni ho hashobora guca haba ibiganiro ku mutekano wa Buraya mu buryo bwagutse."

Ikibazo ni uko Uburaya muri iki gihe butari ku meza y'ibiganiro.

Moscou na yo ntishaka ko bwohabwa ikibanza. Yama inegura abakuru b'ibihugu vya Buraya kubera ubufasha bwa gisirikare baha Kyiv Ubutegetsi bwa Ukraine, hamwe n'ingingo zikomeye bafata ku Burusiya.

Ibiganiro vy'amahoro vyabereye i Abu Dhabi muri Emira Zunze Ubumwe z'Abarabu muri iyi ndwi vyahuje intumwa za Ukraine, Uburusiya na Amerika.

Inyuma y'ibiganiro yagiriye i Moscou, Steve Witkoff yavuze ko Putin yemeye iciyumviro c'uko intumwa za Buraya zokwitaba ibiganiro vy'amahoro biri imbere kuri Ukraine.

Ariko ejo ku wa gatanu, Kremlin yavuze ko ingingo ya nyuma y'uko Uburaya bwohabwa ikibanza muri ivyo biganiro itarafatwa.

Umuvugizi wa Kremlin, Dmitry Peskov, yavuze ati: "Nitwamara gutahura imigambi yabo nyakuri n'ingene biteguriye gufasha mu nzira y'amahoro, ni ho tuzoshobora gufata ingingo ku bijanye n'ibiganiro ku kibazo ca Ukraine mu buryo bwagutse."

None kuri Putin ubwiwe hoho bimeze gute?

Mu biganiro yagiranye na Witkoff na Jared Kushner, yarerekanye ko atarota atezura kandi ko ata kimujugumiza.

Abanyamerika ni bo bariko baramusanga aho yibereye bamusaba amasezerano, mu gihe Abanyaburayi na bo nyene bariko bariyumvira ingene bomushikira. Mu kwezi guheze, abakuru b'ibihugu vya Norvège na Finlande baramuhamagaye kugira bavugane.

Hanyuma kandi mu ndwi iza, i Shenzhen mu Bushinwa, mu nama y'ugufashanya mu vy'ubutunzi mu karere ka Aziya na Pasifika (APEC), Putin ashobora kugirana ibiganiro vyihariye na Donald Trump hamwe na Xi Jinping w'Ubushinwa.

Ibinyamakuru vy'Uburusiya bimaze no kubagereranya n'"Abakuru Batatu" bari bakomeye mu mwaka wa 1945, ari bo Joseph Stalin w'icahoze ari Ubumwe bw'Abasoviyeti, Franklin Roosevelt wa Amerika na Winston Churchill w'Ubwongereza, bahuriye hamwe kugira ngo batunganye gushasha Uburaya inyuma y'Intambara ya Kabiri y'Isi Yose.

Naho biri uko, inyuma y'imyaka hafi itanu y'intambara, Uburusiya bumaze gutakaza ibintu vyinshi ku rugamba.

Ubutunzi bw'Uburusiya na bwo buri ku gitsure kibandanya ciyongera.

N'aho Uburusiya ata gahengwe buha Ukaine, na yo nta gahengwe ibuha mu kubandanya ibitero vyayo vy'indege zitajamwo abadereva ku nganda zitunganya igitoro, ibi bikongereza ubwoba bw'uko hashobora gusubira kuba ikena ry'igitoro.

Ariko gushika ubu, nta kintu na kimwe muri ivyo kirashobora kugondoza Vladimir Putin ngo yemera guhagarika intambara.

The seized money has been deposited into the country's national treasury

Nearly $20m (£14.8m) in cash has been found hidden in farm buildings and buried in forests as part of an investigation into a former minister of Viktor Orbán, authorities have said.

Miklós Seszták, who served as minister of national development for four of the ex-prime minister's 16-year rule, is accused of accepting bribes as part of a scheme involving the state transport company. He has denied any wrongdoing.

Hungary's new Prime Minister Péter Magyar unseated Orbán in a landslide election in April on the promise of launching a sweeping anti-corruption drive.

On Friday, following the two-day search for the cash - found in secluded locations across the country - Magyar described it as the end of the "mafia".

Investigators found wads of banknotes in safes, buried in woodlands and hidden in agricultural and residential buildings and warehouses, as part of the probe into Seszták, the National Asset Recovery and Protection Office (NVVH) said in a statement.

The cash amounted to "5,071,632,000 forints, €2,658,350 and $1,257,100", it added, bringing the combined value to $19.5m. It has been deposited into the Hungarian State Treasury, the body said.

The NVVH was established to investigate allegations of corruption during the Orbán rule, which Magyar has dubbed "Operation Purgatory".

Magyar promised Hungarians "regime change" during the election earlier this year and has set about undoing many Orbán-era policies since entering office.

Allegations of corruption and cronyism have long dogged Orbán, who during the course of his tenure turned Hungary into what the EU characterised as an "electoral autocracy".

Hungarian investigators said they found some of the cash buried in forestry

His government faced accusations of offering lucrative government projects to allies. Orbán has strongly denied the claims.

Two of his former ministers, including Seszták, and the former central bank chief Gyorgy Matolcsy have been under arrest since September over accusations of graft in separate investigations. They all deny wrongdoing.

On Monday, Hungarian authorities also detained Orbán's brother and three others as part of a people-smuggling case.

The former prime minister ​dismissed it as political revenge, saying: "In this dirty game, ​the aim is the elimination of the political opponent and the establishment of a one-party system.

"I am the target, my younger brother is just a tool."

President Emmanuel Macron has flown to Cambodia to flex France’s Global influence through the La Francophonie.

He said, “Our jobs and the future of our regions are defended in France, but also thousands of kilometres from home.”

“In Cambodia, I am coming with business leaders to open up new markets, drawing on the French-speaking world that brings us closer together,” President Macron said on Saturday.

“French expertise and the work already under way are already yielding very tangible opportunities. Cambodia, for example, wants to draw on Rungis’s expertise to create its own wholesale market,” he added.

The French leader is also expected in Malaysia November 16 and 17.

“In Malaysia, I am coming in particular to diversify our supplies of rare earths. We rarely talk about them, yet they are essential to making the magnets used in certain electric motors and electronic devices,” President Macron noted.

He mentioned, “For our factories, having several sources of supply means reducing the risk of having to shut down a production line for lack of parts. It also means being able to invest and produce in France with greater certainty about the future.”

“If we can launch new projects together today with such confidence, it is because others, long before us, learned to work side by side, Macron said.

“At Angkor, that confidence is visible even in the stone. Together with the king, we will inaugurate the restored West Mebon: fourteen years of work by Cambodian and French teams.”

Macron is envisioning, “More partners, less dependence. Our agreements open doors. Language, culture and friendship keep them open. That is good for our countries.”

US negotiators have touted the idea of Ukraine withdrawing its remaining forces from the eastern Donbas region in exchange for Nato membership, Volodymyr Zelensky has said.

The US has not confirmed the Ukrainian president's comments. A US official told the BBC "many ideas continue to be discussed but any final deal will have to be agreed to by both parties".

Zelensky's remarks came after US envoys met him and Russian President Vladimir Putin as part of US efforts to end the war between their two countries.

Kyiv has long sought membership of the military alliance, but this has previously been opposed by the US and others, while Russia has said another Nato member on its border was unacceptable.

Russia launched a full-scale invasion of Ukraine in February 2022 and currently controls most of the industrial Donbas region. Zelensky has consistently said Ukraine was unwilling to give up sovereign territory.

"The Americans raised a question: 'What if Ukraine joins Nato? Would Ukraine withdraw from Donbas?' This was the first time this had been raised," Zelensky said in remarks released by his office on Saturday.

He went on to say that if he received a specific proposal that contained security guarantees, no constraints on Ukraine's military and funds to rebuild the country, he would put it to a referendum.

US envoys Jared Kushner and Steve Witkoff travelled to the Irish capital, Dublin, on Thursday to meet Zelensky, after a round of talks with Putin in Moscow.

Comments by both Putin and Kremlin officials suggest that Russia's position on the war has not shifted. It has previously proposed limits on the size of Ukraine's military, territorial concessions and Kyiv's guaranteed neutrality as conditions of a peace deal.

Ukraine has rejected these suggestions, arguing that such constraints would hamper its ability to stave off any future invasion.

Other Nato members apart from the US are wary of membership for Ukraine - and it is understood that Ukraine itself sees it as unrealistic.

The Kremlin has always been fiercely opposed, too. It is one reason why Russia started this war in the first place.

It is possible the US envoys were exploring Ukraine's "red lines" when it comes to occupied land in the Donbas. Zelensky recently said that the two American mediators believed Kyiv only had to cede territory to achieve peace and were applying pressure, keen to do a deal as soon as possible.

Ukraine is sure that Russia's ambitions are far greater and has long seen Nato as its only sure protection.

So it is also possible that Zelensky made this suggestion public to re-open a discussion that had been considered all but closed.

He said the idea was now "back on the agenda" as part of an "extremely difficult conversation" on European security in his latest remarks.

It also looks like Ukrainian push-back against Russia's renewed hardline stance. Moscow now talks about a "new European security architecture", which is long-standing Russian code for a weaker Nato.

The issue appears to have been the main focus at the latest round of talks between Ukraine, Russia and the US in Abu Dhabi this week.

Hours after Zelensky's remarks, Jared Kushner appeared keen to dampen down any US offer of Nato membership for Ukraine, urging "confidentiality" in a sensitive process.

He said that "maximalist" proposals had been reported from the negotiations, along with "strong political rhetoric".

In what read like a reproach to Kyiv, Kushner referred to "private discussions" aimed at exploring new ideas about ending what he called a "horrible war".

He said the hope was that those ideas might lead to new proposals or breakthroughs.

Russia currently occupies roughly a fifth of Ukrainian territory, including most of the Donetsk and Luhansk regions that compose the Donbas.

It has insisted again that it will not agree to a ceasefire until a final peace deal is in place that would include Ukraine ceding control of those parts of the Donbas Russian troops have not captured, in addition to the Crimean peninsula Moscow annexed illegally in 2014.

The latest round of talks come after a period of fraught relations between Kyiv and Washington over Ukrainian strikes on oil facilities deep inside Russia, which US President Donald Trump had asked Ukraine to pause to facilitate the supply of Russian diesel to ease global fuel prices.

Zelensky then accused US officials of limiting Ukraine's Starlink internet service , which it uses to co-ordinate defensive operations, while Trump said it was "time for Ukraine to get a new president" and called for fresh elections.

Elections are suspended while Ukraine remains under martial law, but Zelensky has previously said he was willing to hold them within months of a peace deal being reached and would give up the presidency in exchange for Nato membership.

King Charles appears in special episode of Elton John's podcast

King Charles and Sir Elton John joked about the problems of ageing as the pair joined for a special radio show to coincide with the monarch's 78th birthday.

Sir Elton, 79, was joined on his regular Rocket Hour radio show for a special episode during which the King shared his musical memories as the pair chose 14 songs together.

The programme also marked the 50th anniversary of the King's Trust and highlighted how musicians have supported the charity's efforts.

"We and the Trust are definitely still standing," the King said, as he highlighted Sir Elton's track I'm Still Standing as one of his favourites because of the song's "message of resilience".

The music legend joked in reply: "I'm still sitting now, though" giving a large laugh, with the King chuckling: "With occasional bits dropping off here and there. I know this is a terrible problem as we get older."

The special was recorded last month at Apple Music Studios in south London and premiered on Saturday morning.

The King recalled Sir Elton's 1986 performance at Wembley Arena, which marked the charity's 10th anniversary.

"I suspect that no-one who was present on that night in 1986 could possibly forget your performance of I'm Still Standing," King Charles said.

"I know people in all kinds of circumstances find this song inspiring, not only for its marvellous spirit, but also its message of resilience. And certainly, 40 years on from that remarkable concert, we and the Trust are definitely still standing."

Sir Elton performed for the 10th anniversary of the King's Trust in 1986 at Wembley Arena

The pair selected a total of 14 tracks. King Charles picked Giant by Calvin Harris and Rag'n'Bone Man, telling Sir Elton that the song summed up his charity because of its message of finding strength from others.

Also selected was Bob Dylan's Gotta Serve Somebody, Muse's Feeling Good and Nectar Woode's Wine into Water, which features Sir Elton on piano.

The Rocket Man star asked the King to highlight a song that he found "extremely meaningful".

Replying that there is "nothing more meaningful than love", the King described an "unforgettable performance" of The Beatles' 1967 hit All You Need is Love by Sir Paul McCartney in 2002 at a concert in honour of Queen Elizabeth II's Golden Jubilee.

"I shall never forget the magic of witnessing a simply unforgettable performance of All You Need Is Love for my late mother's Golden Jubilee at the Party At The Palace concert with Paul McCartney, Rod Stewart and Joe Cocker, and I think with Phil Collins on drums, Brian May and Eric Clapton on guitar and an all-star backing choir," the King said.

"It really is a totally timeless song with a timeless message."

The pair reunited in 2000, where Sir Elton performed alongside the Backstreet Boys at Party in the Park

The show opened with Tina Turner's hit Proud Mary. The King described the late pop icon as an "electrifying character" and recalled that the guard at Buckingham Palace played her hit Simply the Best following her death in 2023.

"It was, I hope, a small way of thanking her for the times she has performed for my charities and indeed for the joy she brought to millions of people," the King said.

The pair also chose Sir Rod Stewart's Handbags And Gladrags, Elvis Presley's Hound Dog, Pete Townsend's Let My Love Open The Door and Raye's Joy.

The programme will be rebroadcast on Apple Music One at 17:00 and 22:00 Saturday and again on Sunday at 02:00 and 06:00. It will also feature on Apple Music Hits on Sunday at 10:00 and 14:00.

Moylan has four goals in six caps for Republic of Ireland

Jack Moylan made his intent clear when speaking to the media in August soon after joining Cardiff City in the summer from Lincoln City.

He outlined how he wanted to impress for the Welsh club and ensure he was a mainstay in Republic of Ireland squads after winning his first two caps in May.

Fast forward three months and the 25-year-old has certainly come good on those promises by stepping up for club and country.

Under fellow Irish man Brian Barry-Murphy at Cardiff he has netted 11 goals in 17 games in all competitions while also providing three assists.

On the international stage, Moylan featured in all four of Republic of Ireland's Nations League games in the extended September/October window, scoring and assisting in a 3-0 win against Israel.

Already a key player for the Bluebirds, Moylan is emerging as an important attacking threat for his country too and will be pivotal in their final two Nations League games against Austria and Kosovo.

It is the latest chapter in the rapid rise of Moylan, who has gone from strength to strength since earning a move to Lincoln in January 2024.

Moylan joined the Imps from Irish Premier Division side Shelbourne after a stellar final season with the Dublin club in which he finished as the league's joint highest scorer with 15 goals.

At the time of the move, he said it was "the next step" in his career and, after an initial bedding in period and two separate spells on the treatment table with an ankle problem, his and Lincoln's form exploded from November 2025 onwards.

The versatile attacker scored 11 goals and provided six assists last season as Lincoln won promotion and beat Cardiff to the League One title.

His impressive campaign led to a first call-up to the Irish senior squad in May and he marked his debut with a hat-trick in a 5-0 win against Grenada before he was sent off in his second game as they drew with Qatar.

Cardiff came calling in the summer and Moylan made the move to Wales on a four-year deal for an undisclosed fee.

He scored the winner on his debut in the EFL Cup against Swindon and three more followed before the first international break, but he has really kicked on since returning to club duty in early October, proving he has adapted to life in the Championship seamlessly.

Moylan, who has featured as a false nine, a number 10 and off the left this season, has seven goals in his last seven league games, including a first-half hat-trick against West Ham with his first goal a fine finish from outside the box.

His boss at club level told BBC Sport Wales in October that Moylan is a "very exciting player to watch because of how attack-minded he is".

Republic of Ireland fans were treated to snippets of those attacking talents in the first four Nations League games.

After coming off the bench in the defeat against Kosovo, Moylan started the next three games, coming in off the right to link well with Troy Parrott and Adam Idah.

He impressed alongside those two players in the comprehensive win over Israel, setting up Idah's goal before racing through and calmly slotting home.

He was a livewire in the draws that followed against Austria and Israel and is in the frame to continue his burgeoning relationship with star striker Parrott, starting with Saturday's trip to Linz to face Austria.

His international boss Heimir Hallgrimsson knew that he had unearthed a gem from the moment Moylan arrived to train with the senior squad for the first time and hopes there is plenty more to come from him in a green shirt.

"Moylan of course has taken the headlines and taken the spotlight the last couple of weeks and hopefully he can transfer that into the national team," he said.

"His rise has been really fast, but that's brilliant when you find someone in the May [friendly] camp, coming in and scoring three goals in his first game and since then he's been involved in the starting 11 more or less.

"Absolute impact from his first game. Sometimes you need up to 10 games to be comfortable at this level, but he was comfortable from the first minute and from the first training session he had a 'wow' impact."

While it is early days with club and his country, the signs are good that Moylan's trajectory is set to continue on the upward curve it has been trending at over the last two years.

Northern Ireland are top of Nations League Group B2 with eight points from four games

Before this Nations League campaign, Northern Ireland had won just one of 16 games played in the second tier of the competition.

But after eight points from four games across September and October, all without conceding a goal, Michael O'Neill's side could end Saturday night as a League A side for the first time.

For that to come to pass, Hungary would need to lose to Georgia in Tbilisi [17:00 GMT] before a Northern Ireland win at home to Ukraine in the later kick-off.

Even if only they hold up their end of the bargain with a win at Windsor Park, the side would travel to Budapest on Tuesday night knowing a point would be good enough to top the group and seal promotion.

"You do look at the teams that do step up and it's tough. We've seen teams do that before and they find it very difficult," said O'Neill after stressing his side would be looking no further than the first game of this double-header.

"But for us to get that opportunity to play against those big teams in a competitive group stage would be great, it would be great for the development of the team.

"I wouldn't say the results at that point wouldn't be important, but I think we'd learn a lot."

Strong performance in the Nations League carries multiple rewards.

Finishing in the top two of their group - something Northern Ireland would confirm with a draw against Ukraine - would ensure O'Neill's side are among the second group of seeds when the draw for Euro 2028 qualifying is made in Belfast next month.

There is also the potential backdoor route into the qualification play-offs too, the same method used by Northern Ireland to find themselves just two games from the summer's World Cup despite finishing third in their group.

But for O'Neill promotion would also bring the less tangible benefit of showing his squad what is required to reach the very top.

O'Neill has previously sought out friendlies against the likes of Spain and France, drawing praise from his then Les Bleus counterpart Didier Deschamps for taking a game against the latter on the eve of the World Cup when others had not been so keen.

Midfielder Shea Charles previously spoke of how going up against the likes of Spain's Rodri in such fixtures helped "prepare" him for the Premier League before he got his £30m move to Fulham.

And O'Neill feels further exposure to such challenges, especially in regular competitive fixtures, would be hugely beneficial to others in his largely inexperienced side.

He added: "That's good for any player, but particularly young players, because it lets them see what's required, what's required to be a Spanish international and playing in the Champions League or playing your club football at the highest level in Europe.

"We want our players to aspire to try to get there too."

Barnsley midfielder Patrick Kelly scored his first international goal in that game against France, the strike coming on a night he shared the field with the likes of Kylian Mbappe, Ousmane Dembele and Michael Olise.

The 22-year-old, who joined the Tykes in the summer of 2025 having not made a senior appearance for West Ham, has played all his club football in either League One, League Two, or the Irish Premiership.

"Playing those bigger nations, it would only improve us as a team," he said.

"You want to test yourself against the best. A couple of the lads have experienced it, they would have played Germany in the last [qualifying] campaign and done well, and I had it that night against France.

"Playing against the best players in the world, you see where you're at and the team as well."

Having missed that game against France through suspension, Blackburn Rovers defender Tom Atcheson's only international start coming into this campaign had been against Guinea, but the 20-year-old senses the team is ready for the step up.

"I think we do belong there and we're showing it," he said. "We want to have those challenges, we want to challenge ourselves against the best because it's exciting times.

"We know what we're capable of. To get into League A with those massive nations would be unbelievable, that's where we all want to get.

"We're looking forward to the next two games and hopefully to make that happen."

MN202611_1jynghifdw4.t:
England are three points behind Spain at the top of their Nations League group

Manager Thomas Tuchel will remind England's players of Uefa's anti-racism protocols before Sunday's Nations League fixture against Spain in Madrid.

The match will be England's first in the Spanish capital since a notorious fixture at Real Madrid's Bernabeu stadium in 2004 which was overshadowed by racist chanting aimed at England players.

The Spanish federation was fined last month and ordered to play their next friendly match with a partial stadium closure after fans sang "Islamophobic and xenophobic" chants about Muslims during a game against Egypt.

"We had a same discussion before the Serbia game [in Belgrade in September 2025]," Tuchel said. "There is a protocol in place.

"Maybe we take our five minutes to inform the players about the protocol if there is a precedent [in Madrid]."

European governing body Uefa, the organiser of the Nations League, has a three-step protocol to handle incidents of discrimination inside stadiums, designed to give referees the power to halt matches, and even abandon games if racist behaviour continues.

In the first instance, referees halt the match and request an announcement on the public address system.

Then, if discrimination continues, officials can stop the game for five to 10 minutes and take the players from the field.

If issues continue after the second stoppage, then the game can be abandoned.

"It's important that the players know about the protocol," Tuchel said.

"And then, yeah, we will give our answers if stuff like this happens. Best answers are on the pitch."

Who would make your England-Spain combined XI?

England's black players such as Ashley Cole and Rio Ferdinand were subject to racist chanting during the 2004 friendly in Madrid

Sunday's fixture takes place at Atletico Madrid's home, the Metropolitano.

Victory would ensure England win their Nations League group and earn a more favourable quarter-final draw but world champions Spain are unbeaten in 43 matches, including a 3-2 win at Wembley in September.

"It's important that we play with the same mindset that we played at home, and attack them and try to make it a physical game, and try to impose our strength," Tuchel added.

"It [Spain] is a team that has forgotten how to lose, so it requires a top performance first of all, and if we can deliver this performance, it will give us a big boost.

"I think we're there, and I think we're ready to win on Sunday,"

MN202611_rmr70jj4f5.t:
Nigel Clough took charge of Mansfield Town in November 2020

Becoming the longest-serving manager at a club takes some doing in the fickle world of football.

Sticking around at two clubs long enough to hold that mantle is just about unprecedented.

But Mansfield Town's Nigel Clough is about to redefine longevity as a manager when it comes to working at sides that make up the top 92 in the English pyramid.

"I don't think it's particularly an achievement; I think it's more an indictment of football that nobody else has lasted that long," Clough told BBC Sport.

This weekend he becomes the longest-serving manager – in terms of active years in the job and league matches at the helm – of the Stags, where he surpasses club great Ian Greaves.

The 16 years Clough spent at Burton Albion, which took in around 900 matches across two spells spanning more than two decades, means the record at the east Staffordshire side is already his.

Former England forward Clough is now six years and one week into the Stags job and is the second longest-serving manager across England's top four leagues - behind only Mikel Arteta at Arsenal - but he does not see his staying power as anything special.

"I don't really think about it that much, I have to say. I'm just trying to get through the week," said Clough, who has been in charge of Mansfield for 329 matches across all competitions.

While Clough's players, as well as Mansfield fans have a different take on what his lengthy tenure at the One Call Stadium has meant, the 60-year-old reeled off the names of legendary past managers - his late father and iconic Nottingham Forest boss Brian Clough included - when reflecting on what joy clubs would have by sticking by their manager.

"When you look back 20 or 30 years, my dad was at Forest for 18 years, Alex Ferguson was at Manchester United for so long and then there was Arsene Wenger at Arsenal. That was at the top level, but even lower down there was a lot of managers who stayed a lot of years," he said

"I just think it's sad the way football is going at the moment. The first bad period that people have, a month, two months or something like that, and the manager is the one that goes."

Clough, who played in the top flight for Forest, Liverpool and Manchester City, has been in management for 28 years and been in charge of just four clubs - Mansfield, Burton, Derby County and Sheffield United - in that time.

Since bounding from non-league level - where he spent the first 10 years of his management career in his first spell at Burton - to take the reins of Derby in the Championship in 2009, no-one has overseen more matches than Clough's 893 across England's top four divisions.

The latest statistics from the League Managers' Association show that managers across those leagues are now staying in their jobs for less than a year on average.

Clough bucking the trend with his record-setting endurance at Mansfield comes in the same week that Manchester United sacked Michael Carrick, when he was 10 months into the job, and Crystal Palace relieved Pierre Sage of his role after only 16 games.

When asked if Clough has ever felt his job was under threat during any "sticky period" at Mansfield, he responded with a firm "of course".

It was when the Stags were in the relegation places and on a 12-match winless run in his first full campaign in charge in 2021-22.

He survived that, then oversaw a club-record 11 consecutive home wins and went on to guide Mansfield to the League Two play-off final at Wembley later the same season.

"You've got to go through that period and you've got to get through it," Clough said of dealing with difficult runs as a manager.

"And I think as you get a little bit older, you know more that it's going to change.

"You get a result out of adversity as much as anything. If you're winning, it doesn't keep going, and if you're losing it's the same thing if you've got a reasonable team and you're doing the right things."

Clough: 'Six years have gone extremely quickly'

Mansfield boss Clough on 25 years 'in family business'

Nigel Clough's Mansfield side are 11th in the League One table after 13 games this season

While Mansfield missed out on promotion when they took their bid all the way to the national stadium in 2022, they went up automatically two years later when they finished third in the table.

It ended Mansfield's 21-year absence from the third tier. And when he kept them up in their first season back, Clough did what no-one had done for 35 years.

Last season they finished 10th, the club's highest league placing since 1987 when Greaves guided them to exactly the same position in the standings.

Stags supporter Dean Foulkes says it "has been an incredible journey" at Mansfield since Clough took the helm in November 2020.

At Burton he is a club legend for the way he transformed the Brewers as a non-league side in his first spell there before taking them to the Championship during his second stint.

He leapt a number of divisions when he left Burton the first time to manage Derby - a particularly poignant job as his father took the Rams to their first English title in 1972.

Even at Sheffield United, where Clough had the shortest stint of his managerial career, he guided them to the semi-final of the FA Cup when they were a League One side in 2014.

"He is really good football man to have around. We should be proud that he is Mansfield Town manager," Foulkes told BBC Radio Nottingham.

"Look at what he has achieved, promotion, and we now have players coming to Mansfield Town because they want to play for Nigel Clough."

It is why prolific veteran forward David McGoldrick moved there in the summer, and how the club has enticed former Leeds United forward Tyler Roberts, as well as ex-Preston forward Michael Smith to the Nottinghamshire town while also landing highly-rated Tottenham midfielder George Abbott on loan.

Ryan Sweeney says the chance to play for Clough was "the main reason" he decided to return to the club last summer.

Former Nottingham Forest and Southend striker Stephen McLaughlin says Clough "manages differently to any other manager" he has worked with.

"He doesn't treat you as a number, he treats you as a person and you want to run though bricks walls for him," McLaughlin said.

"It's hard to explain what he does for you on and off the pitch as well. You are not on the grass too long in training because he trusts you to get your work in and to be ready for Saturday.

"He doesn't give too much tactical information to people because the message is 'just do your job and work hard'."

Jordan Bowery has been asked to do that more than most, having been transformed from a striker to a defender and is now seen as 'Mr Versatile'. , external

"He is incredibly loyal and trusts me in those positions," Bowery said. "A lot of managers wouldn't do that, but he's had my back and I appreciate that.

"He can get onto you, but that is like most managers. He expects and demands the best out of every single one of you each day.

"He has obviously been around the game a long time, played at the highest level - he knows the game and he knows the players."

A young Nigel Clough (right) pictured in 1978, sat alongside his father Brian in the Nottingham Forest dugout

And Clough, the player, is a former attacker of considerable repute in Nottinghamshire.

No-one has scored more than Clough's 131 goals for Forest over the past 113 years.

It was there, at Mansfield's high-profile county neighbours, where he thrived under his father who famously guided the Reds to the First Division title in 1978 before collecting back-to-back European Cups.

The manager that Clough is has been shaped by the successes he watched up close as a child and those he later revelled in as a player.

"When you're brought up in the household that we were brought up in and the environment we were brought up in, then we have a certain insight into what it takes to have a chance of being successful and what you expect of the team and everything," he said.

"And the empathy, I don't think you should ever forget that if you've been a player as well, how that feels when you have a rough time and so on."

And it is those players, and how they are found before investing in them that is the closest thing to revealing the secret to Clough's longevity.

"We don't like wasting the owners' money," he said.

"Whether it was at Burton when we were in the Dr Martens South [non-league level] or whether it's here at Mansfield Town, we try and look after it as best we can. And we have a responsibility to do that.

"We do as much in-depth research as we can on players. Character is the main feature of what we look at. We can see all the stuff on the videos of what they can do, then we watch them live and everything, but you have to delve really into the character and get a lot of references from players, coaches, managers.

"We take that very seriously. Each season we set out to just try and get a few better players in the squad.

"It's keeping the ball rolling, keeping the owners happy, keeping the supporters happy."

Additional reporting by BBC Radio Nottingham's David Jackson and Jake Garner.

Abantu bababa 130 bari mu bwato bw'ingenzi bwari buhagaze ku kivuko i New Orleans bose bashoboye gutabarwa bararokoka inyuma y'aho bugongewe n'ubwato butwara igitoro.

Ubwo bwato, American Heritage, bwatembagariye mu ruzi Mississippi buryamira urubavu, inyuma y'uko bugonzwe n'ubwato butwara imizigo, Atlantic Asphalt.

Abantu 32 bari muri ubwo bwato bwagonzwe bajanywe kwa muganga bakomeretse bukebuke, ariko nta n'umwe yaburiwe irengero. Abategetsi bati: "Ni igitangaro kuri Mississippi".

Naho igituma nyaco cateje iyi mpanuka kitaramenyekana, Kapiteni Melanie Burnham arongoye ingabo zicungera inkengera z'ibahari yavuze ko hari ibimenyetso vyerekana ko ubwo bwato bushobora kuba bwaragize ikibazo c'i vola (volant/ steering).

Umukuru w'igisagara ca New Orleans, Helena Moreno, yabwiye abanyamakuru ko ari ugushima ku gikorwa nyamukuru c'ubutabazi cakozwe n'abajetwe ubutabazi ba mbere "baciye bihutira gufasha mu bubangutsi ntangere".

Yagize ati: "Nta muntu n'umwe yaburiwe irengero, kandi mu vy'ukuri iki ni igitangaro kuri Mississippi."

Melanie Montroll, umukuru w'Ikivuko ca New Orleans, yavuze ko amakuru y'iyo mpanuka yatanguye gushika nk'isaha indwi n'igice z'umutaga (13:30) mu masaha y'ako karere, ni ukuvuga (isaha zibiri n'igice, 20h30, mu masaha ya Gitega na Kigali) ejo ku wa gatanu, abantu baca batangura kugerageza gufasha abari muri ubwo bwato bwari bwatanguye kwinjiramwo amazi.

Uburongozi bw'iki kivuko buvuga ko bwarimwo ingenzi zishika 129 hamwe n'abakozi babwo igihe iyo mpanuka yaba.

Ubwo bwato bwariko burarangiza urugendo rw'imisi umunani rwaciye mu bibanza bitandukanye biri ku ruzi Mississippi mu ntara za Louisiana na Mississippi.

Perezida Donald Trump yanditse ku rubuga nyagiro rwa Truth Social ko ico gikorwa co gutabara cari "igikorwa c'agatangaza".

Umushikiranganji w'Umutekano mu gihugu, Markwayne Mullin, yavuze ko abajejwe gucungera inkengera na bo nyene bafashije mu bikorwa vy'ubutabazi.

Buramatari Jeff Landry na we nyene yavuze ko ubwo butabazi ari "igitangaro kuri Mississippi" uravye "igitigiri kinini c'abari muri ubwo bwato" bose barokotse.

Landry yavuze ko ingendo z'amato zimaze imyaka myinshi ata gatosi ku ruzi Mississippi, akaba yiyemeje gukora amatohoza yimbitse kugira icateye iyo mpanuka kimenyekane.

Umwe mu babonye iryo sanganya yabwiye CBS, ikimenyeshamakuru gikorana na BBC muri Amerika, ati: "Wamengo ni filime y'intambara. Iyumvire nawe amatoni menshi y'ivyuma asekanye. Ni ko vyari bimeze. Vyasa nk'ivyabaye kuri Titanic."

Yavuze ko yabonye ingenzi n'abakozi b'ubwato bariko basemerera, barira, mu kugerageza kuva muri ubwo bwato igihe bwariko buribira mu mazi.

Nk'uko bigaragara ku rubuga rwabwo, ubwato American Heritage bushobora gutwara ingenzi zishika 150, kandi burimwo inzu y'ibiyo yo gufunguriramwo, ikigo c'imyimenyerezo ngororamubiri hamwe n'ivyumba bitatu ingenzi ziruhukiramwo.

Bwubatswe mu mwaka wa 2015 kandi bufise nibura amagorofa ane.

An appeal on protecting cultural heritage and promoting cultural diversity is scheduled to be adopted during the Francophonie Summit in Phnom Penh, Cambodia Foreign Affairs Ministry has said.

The appeal follows severe damage to UNESCO-listed Temple of Preah Vihear after it was bombed during last year’s border clashes between Cambodia and Thailand.

For Cambodia, the damage at Preah Vihear illustrates what heritage protection entails after fighting. UNESCO documented extensive damage to the temple during the July and December 2025 clashes.

During the December fighting, UNESCO urged all parties to protect cultural heritage and reminded them of their obligations under the 1954 Hague Convention for the Protection of Cultural Property in the Event of Armed Conflict and the 1972 World Heritage Convention.

The organisation said it had shared the locations of World Heritage sites and sites of national significance with the parties concerned to help prevent damage.

The Phnom Penh Appeal on the Protection of Cultural Heritage and the Promotion of Cultural Diversity is one of three documents expected to emerge from the November 15–16 summit, the first Cambodia has hosted, and just the second to be held in Asia.

The other two are the Phnom Penh Declaration, which will address peaceful coexistence and cooperation, and a resolution on crisis response, recovery and peacebuilding in the Francophonie.

The world is anxiously waiting for a verdict on whether Myanmar committed genocide against its marginalised Muslim Rohingya minority.

The International Court of Justice (ICJ) is scheduled to convene on Thursday.

Rohingya activists say the pending judgement should haunt the minds of ASEAN leaders when they meet in the Philippines starting Sunday.

“We are waiting to see what the outcome will be on that day, the judgement for everything we have been experiencing for generations,” said a 25-year-old Yangon-based Rohingya activist who requested anonymity for security reasons.

“If they welcome people who lack basic humanity and destroyed our lives, our futures and our possessions, we will be very let down,” he added.

The Hague case dates back to 2017, when Myanmar is accused of breaching the United Nations Genocide Convention by brutalising the Rohingya.

The judgement due Thursday will weigh state culpability, not individual guilt.

Myanmar’s military chief Min Aung Hlaing led the military as it spearheaded the mass killings, rape and arson targeting the Rohingya and driving nearly 750,000 into Bangladesh as refugees.

In April, Min Aung Hlaing was installed as president after elections.

ASEAN bloc members are carefully waiting for the ICJ ruling which could change their relations with Myanmar.

The Association of Southeast Asian Nations (ASEAN) are scheduled to meet on Sunday(Nov15-17) in the Philippines.

On the summit agenda delegates will debate a policy of freezing Myanmar out of summits since a 2021 putsch.

Highlights: Scotland 2-1 North Macedonia

As Scotland legend Kenny Dalglish watched one of his records equalled in Scotland's 2-1 win over North Macedonia, another of his feats loomed into view.

The night was supposed to be about Andy Robertson joining Dalglish as Scotland's most-capped man, the Tottenham left-back making his 102nd appearance for his country.

But instead, for the first time, the 75-year-old might be nervous that his crown as one of Scotland men's all-time top goalscorers is wobbling.

That is because, in Scotland's rather humdrum Nations League victory, John McGinn - in his 94th Scotland appearance - took two big strides towards the record.

The Aston Villa midfielder now has 24 goals for his country - six shy of Dalglish's long-standing record of 30, shared with Denis Law.

"It's something that's been in the back of my head," McGinn admitted in the post-match debrief. "If I start climbing that table, it means we've been successful as a team."

Now 32 years old, time is running out for him. But as he pulls level with Hughie Gallacher, one of the Wembley Wizards of folklore, his ambition is clear.

McGinn double gives drab Scotland win over North Macedonia

There was a time when talk of this record being toppled seemed laughable. Scotland has produced strikers in recent decades, but none close to Dalglish or Law.

The fact a midfielder might take the title makes McGinn's feat all the more astonishing.

His prowess in front of goal is no secret to the Tartan Army. There was the spell at the end of 2019 where he scored six in three games, his overhead kick against Austria, his late winner against Croatia in 2024.

But of late, his lack of goals and even his performances have had some fans questioning where he fits into the Scotland team.

"It has been a bit of a dry patch for me over the last year on the goal front," McGinn admitted, and he's not wrong.

He failed to find the back of the net for Scotland in 2025, the first time he'd done that since 2020.

But, just as his form at Villa has sky-rocketed, he came up big for his new international head coach Sebastien Pocognoli.

"Isn't it great to have a John McGinn in your team?" former Scotland winger Pat Nevin said on Sportsound. "He's somebody you'd want to have in your team to be taking a penalty for you.

"I'd be surprised if John McGinn doesn't get the goal record now. It might take him another year or two, but he is definitely capable of getting that record."

Becoming Scotland's main penalty taker will help, a fact McGinn alluded to coyly post-match.

In his career, he had only taken one spot-kick before this season - scoring for Scotland in the 3-3 draw against Norway back in 2023.

In this campaign he has scored three and missed one, smacking the bar against Fulham on Halloween.

In classic McGinn fashion, he bounced back to slot home against Manchester United the following week, before being caught on ref-cam admitting to the official that he was nervous to take it after his hitting the woodwork.

That jovial, lovable personality has not just won him fans off the pitch. It is clear that his team-mates at both Villa and the national team adore him.

"He's not going to stop until he [gets the record]," said striker Che Adams, who helped set up McGinn's first against North Macedonia.

"Everyone's pleased for him, he's the best person I've met in football. For him to get the recognition he deserves is amazing."

McGinn's iconic status in Scottish football is secure and will not be tarnished if he fails to climb the mountain.

Whether it is calling Scotland performances 'jobby', or admitting he would "probably be at Yeovil" were it not for his backside, the midfielder has already won the heart of a nation.

The 48th session of the Ministerial Conference of La Francophonie (CMF) opened today in the Cambodian capital Phnom Penh.

According to a line up of to-do things, the ministers are examining several political and cooperation issues, as well as draft texts to be submitted to heads of state and government.

The Ministerial conference is being chaired by H.E. Prak Sokhonn, Deputy Prime Minister of Cambodia.

It precedes the 20th Summit of Francophonie, scheduled for November 15 and 16 in the Cambodian capital.

The conference is examining the draft Phnom Penh Declaration and a resolution on crisis response and peace consolidation in the French-speaking world.

During the conference, Cambodia called for discussions on protecting cultural heritage and promoting cultural diversity, as well as the future of digital technology and artificial intelligence for young people and the economy.

Conference delegates are also discussing the appointment of the CMF vice-president and adopt the reports of the 46th CMF session in Kigali in 2025 and the 47th extraordinary CMF session in Paris in 2026.

The conference is also exploring items including communications from associate members and observer states and governments, multilateral Francophone cooperation, and the OIF’s administrative and financial matters.

The conference will also decide the date and venue of the next Ministerial Conference of La Francophonie.

MN202611_17a08b4t4ry.t:
Plants and trees from hotter parts of the world are being brought into Sussex

Gardeners in one of the most drought-hit parts of the UK have said they are adapting their planting strategies amid increasingly extreme weather.

West Sussex - like most of the country - experienced an unprecedented summer marked by record-breaking heatwaves and severe drought.

The conditions have put immense stress on many traditional plant species, with some seriously struggling or dying completely.

Iain Parkinson, head of landscape and horticulture at Kew Wakehurst near Ardingly, said he had seen a "big change" in climate over the some 40 years he has worked there.

Meanwhile, senior gardener at High Beeches near Haywards Heath, Elliot Chandler, said some rhododendrons had died off this year.

"That's probably going to continue," he said.

"We'll do what we can for the plants...but if they're not surviving, then we need to plant different things.

"That's the only way we can really maintain the garden and keep it full of interest and flowers."

This year's heat and lack of rainfall were unprecedented

Joe Whelan, head gardener at Nymans in Handcross, warned another year of drought could be "quite detrimental" on larger, more mature trees.

The gardeners said planting a greater diversity of species will be key to climate resilience, with plants from North America, southeastern Europe, central Asia, South Korea and Japan potentially faring better in future.

Chandler added it will not be a case of ripping out old plants and planting new species "in one go" but rather a gradual change over time with a "really diverse mix of things".

Whelan said it will be difficult to predict what will do well in the future.

It will be about "experimenting and accepting that some things probably aren't going to make it", he continued.

Country music superstar Garth Brooks will perform a multi-city tour of Ireland in 2027

Fans of Garth Brooks will be brushing off their Stetsons and polishing their cowboy boots after the country music superstar announced he will be performing in multiple cities across Ireland in 2027.

The tour includes Belfast, Galway, Kilkenny, Limerick and Cork and will be the first time he has played in Northern Ireland since his King's Hall gig in November 1998.

The singer has said in the past that Ireland is his favourite place in the world to sing , and the love appears to be mutual as his first two Belfast concerts sold out, with an extra date already added.

So why has an American country music star remained so popular with Irish fans for so many years?

Cathy O'Reilly previously saw Garth Brooks live at two of his Dublin concerts in 2022

Cathy O'Reilly, who is originally from County Monaghan but lives in Belfast, managed to get her tickets for the very first show of Garth Brooks' tour on 21 May 2027 at Boucher Road Playing Fields.

She has already seen Brooks perform live before - twice during his run of concerts in Dublin in 2022 and her love of his music was passed on from her parents and uncles.

"It's growing up listening to him it brings me back to my childhood. My uncle gave me his cd, he didn't even buy me one - just gave me his because I loved him so much."

She believes the Irish link to the US and the fact that fans on the island give the best welcome to performers, are the reasons for Garth Brooks' popularity in Ireland.

"He [Garth Brooks] gives us energy and we're giving it back ten-fold nearly, and we're just so welcoming so he really enjoys coming here."

Garth Brooks last performed in Ireland in 2022

Peter Aiken, from Aiken Promotions, told Irish broadcaster RTÉ that the new Belfast gig is "red hot".

"There could be a fourth show in Belfast," he said.

Brooks is the biggest selling artist in US history and is the only artist to pass 200 million albums sold.

In 2014 about 400,000 fans booked tickets to five concerts he had planned for Dublin's Croke Park but Dublin City Council only granted permission for three of them.

Brooks said he would only perform all five concerts or none at all and so the shows were cancelled.

He returned to Dublin in September 2022.

Stephen Butler performs as a Garth Brooks tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls and described his job as "easy" due to the love of Garth Brooks' fans

Stephen Butler from Newtownabbey performs as a Garth Brooks' tribute act with the band Thunder Rolls.

His love for the musician also goes back to his childhood.

"My mother was a fan when I was younger, she was always playing his music and buying his albums so I loved the songs.

"I knew, with me loving Garth and there being such a following in Ireland, I knew it was the right thing to do."

He went to the Dublin concert in 2022 and while he hasn't yet got tickets for the Ireland dates next year, he hopes to get tickets to at least one of them closer to the time.

Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music"

"I was able to get four or five tickets about a week or two before the Croke Park shows, I'll definitely go - I have to go.

"His band is amazing, he's amazing, and his songs - he's got an endless amount of anthems."

Butler said in order to embody the stage persona of Garth Brooks, you "have to be passionate about his music".

"I'm not saying I'm as good as Garth Brooks, but I definitely have his enthusiasm.

"I talk about him and how much I love him throughout the songs and I just identify with them as much as I can.

"My job is easy, I just have to go on there and get everybody singing along with me."

Garth Brooks performing at the King's Hall in 1998

Butler says he thinks the reason Garth Brooks remains so enduringly popular in Ireland is because the people here identify so strongly with his songs.

"Everybody loves Friends In Low Places, people of Ireland love it, they love Callin' Baton Rouge.

"I speak to a lot of people after I play the shows and a lot of people identify with some of the words in the songs, they tell me about a relative that's passed and they seem to have some kind of identification with the songs Tomorrow Never Comes or Unanswered Prayers - it talks about love and about how Garth feels.

"And in amongst Thunder Rolls and the big hits that Garth has, he sings big rocky country rock and ballads, so it's exciting and it's sad - it's an emotional roller coaster," he said.

"And he's such a down-to-earth, genuine, caring person, he seems to be a good soul and I think people people identify with his personality.

"It's a big working-class country and they love someone that's genuine and that talks from the heart."
