MN202611_1xhdjt76ga1.t:
Declan spent almost seven weeks cycling from the west coast of America to the east coast

Declan Faulkner and his wife Patrina always intended to return to the United States, a place they visited shortly after getting married almost 30 years ago, and maybe make a cross-country trip.

But, as is sometimes the case, life had other plans.

They moved close to Patrina's home village of Ballygawley, County Tyrone, developed their careers, raised three children – and then Patrina was diagnosed with breast cancer. Four years later, in 2017, she died.

But Declan never forgot the journey they were meant to take together – which is why the 55-year-old just spent seven weeks cycling coast-to-coast across the US, from Portland, Oregon on the west coast to Portland, Maine.

Declan's wife Patrina died in April 2017

"When things got tough throughout the journey, I just had Patrina's voice in my head and I dug deep thinking about what she and other cancer patients go through," he said, reflecting on one of the hardest but more rewarding challenges of his life.

It was during Patrina's illness that Declan found an outlet in the form of endurance sports, setting him on a path to his 3,800-mile (6,115km) epic cycle across the US.

"I've always been a keen runner and love to cycle, and even when she was sick Patrina would give me the green light to go off to the Mourne mountains for the day," he said.

"I just loved the serenity of running and cycling there and I suppose mentally it really helped me hold things together at the time.

"I'd remembered talking to Patrina about this idea I had in my head of going back to America and cycling coast to coast.

"Ten years had passed since she died and the kids have grown up, and I just thought wouldn't it be great to see America on two wheels with the memory of Patrina on my shoulder along the way."

Declan said he loved the serenity of running and cycling

So at 55 years old, Declan, who is a financial adviser by day, decided to take a short career break to fulfil a lifelong dream, while raising cancer awareness along the way.

He was joined on the road by his friend from Cork, Donncha O'Brien, another keen cyclist.

Declan said: "We had met a few years back on cycling trip in Kerry and had become great friends and thank God he was there because he kept pushing me.

"There were days when you felt like your body was just shutting down and you were sore all over, because we were spending sometimes 10 hours a day on the bikes without a break."

The men spent 43 days on their bike and averaged 85 miles (137km) a day, but on some days cycled up to 120 miles (193km).

They cycled 45,000m of elevation, the equivalent of five-and-a-half Mount Everests.

The journey took them through some of the most spectacular landscapes in North America - over the Big Horn Mountains in Wyoming and along the Great Lakes.

Among the spectacular places Declan passed through was Yellowstone National Park

Declan said he had several pinch-me moments throughout the trip.

He said: "Cycling into Devil's Tower, Wyoming, which I think was one of the first national parks inaugurated in 1906 and it's just this big volcanic plug - we cycled there on a beautiful day.

"Seeing that for the first time was special.

"Then coming into Vermont in the autumn and some of the colours of the trees were just stunning.

"And we cycled through this amazing lightning storm in upstate New York in the dark, with the lightning strikes just lighting up the whole place."

There were also many hard days along the way too.

"Cycling through the strongest winds I've ever experienced in South Dakota was probably the toughest.

"Leaving South Dakota Badlands National Park we actually ran out of water and my sugar levels just dropped and I nearly fell of my bike a number of times, I was just exhausted."

The gruelling journey involved storms, strong winds and much-needed breaks by the roadside

Declan's journey started at the Pacific Ocean and ended at the Atlantic Ocean.

He says seeing the Atlantic coast is something he will never forget.

"Our final destination was this beach right on the Atlantic Ocean, and the last 20 miles to it just went in a flash, and taking the bikes down to the water on that last day was totally surreal.

"I wasn't overly emotional until that evening when a friend sent me a picture of Patrina and I from 30 years ago when we were at a party at college.

"That just brought the tears because I was looking at that picture and felt like she was with me the entire way."

As part of the cycle, Declan raised almost £20,000 for Charis Cancer Care, which runs a specialist care centre on the banks of Lough Fea in County Tyrone where Patrina spent many days after her diagnosis.

Arlene McAvoy from Charis Cancer Care praised Declan for his achievement

The centre in the foothills of the Sperrin Mountains, just outside Cookstown, provides a free-of-charge service offering emotional, physical and practical support to people with cancer.

Arlene McAvoy from the charity said: "With Declan doing this cycle in Patrina's memory and raising awareness, it's just amazing what he has achieved.

"Each year we have about 1,400 people who come to our centre.

"It's not just for the person who is going through cancer, but it's also for their families and carers as well, and I know this was a special place for Declan also."

Reaching the Atlantic coast was an unforgettable moment for Declan

Now that Declan is back home, he says it is taking a bit of getting used to.

He added: "You wake up thinking: Have I pumped the tyres? Have I greased the pedals? Are the lights charged?'

"It's mad because you've been in that cycling bubble for so long.

"But now that I'm looking back on it, I am very proud, and I do think about what Patrina would think.

"She'd probably laugh and say: 'You're not wise' - but I know she'd be proud too."

MN202611_1o3qwwriubd.t:
Sonia Bompastor was working as Lyon's head of youth development when Melvine Malard played at Clairfontaine

Thousands of miles from home, a 14-year-old had an encounter that would change her life.

Nestled in a forest about an hour from Paris is France's national football academy at Clairefontaine. Famous for developing global stars such as Kylian Mbappe and Thierry Henry, it is also where a teenage Melvine Malard first met Sonia Bompastor in 2014.

Malard had travelled from Reunion Island, a French overseas territory in the Indian Ocean, to play in a football tournament. Watching from the sidelines was a titan of French football.

Bompastor, a two-time Champions League winner who had become Lyon's head of youth development, spotted the young forward and persuaded her to move to mainland France.

Twelve years later, the pair have been reunited at Chelsea. After joining from Manchester United in July, Malard has already established herself as a key player.

It took just six appearances for the 26-year-old to match her six-goal tally from last season's Women's Super League, helping fill the void left by Sam Kerr's departure.

"I knew she had the potential to be a really good player," Bompastor tells BBC Sport. "Having known her for so long and all the hard work she has put in, I'm really proud of her."

Convincing Malard's mother to let her daughter move nearly 6,000 miles from home was not straightforward - but Bompastor had a plan for the phone call.

"It's a lot of responsibility for you as a coach to bring a young player like this and move her from her own family," Bompastor says.

"The main thing for her mum in that phone call was she knew she could trust me as a manager but also as a woman."

For teenager Malard, the transition was difficult. She was close to her family and struggled with the bitterly cold winters of Lyon.

Because of its tropical climate, temperatures on Reunion Island rarely drop below 20C even in winter, whereas in Lyon, the mercury remains in low single figures during December and January.

Bompastor still laughs about one particular conversation with the young forward.

"She said to me: 'I'm so sorry, Sonia, but I think I need to go back to my place. It's so cold here. I can't play football any more!'" says Bompastor.

But Malard stuck around, knowing the opportunity was too good to turn down.

"When Lyon calls you, it's maybe just one time in your life," she says. "So you need to take your opportunity when it comes."

Bompastor's influence extended beyond football. As head of Lyon's academy, she also kept a close eye on Malard's education.

"When I did bad in school, she called me," Malard says. "'Mel, where are you? The school called me - it's not good what you're doing!'

"That was a nightmare - Sonia is always here."

Their relationship continued as Malard progressed through the ranks and finally broke into Lyon's first team as a 17-year-old in 2017.

By the time Bompastor had become the club's head coach for the 2021-22 season, Malard had established herself in the team and at the end of that campaign, she started the Champions League final against Barcelona as Bompastor's side secured a 3-1 victory.

For the boss, it remains a particularly special memory.

"When you look at all the journey and Melvine coming as a young kid into a different environment, far away from her family... and how she improved to be starting that game and for us to win that game," Bompastor says. "It's a big achievement."

Title race hots up before Chelsea-Man City showdown

Cast your vote for BBC Women's Footballer of the Year 2026

Chelsea have had 13 different goalscorers in the WSL this season with Malard's six topping the list

Now reunited with her former boss at Chelsea, Malard has relished the responsibility of leading the line following Kerr's departure.

It took her just 341 minutes to chalk up six league goals for her new club. Last season, despite scoring four in the first two games, it was 17 matches and 1,206 minutes before she hit the same number for Manchester United.

Goals have come alongside frequently getting into dangerous positions.

At United in 2025-26, she averaged 3.4 shots and 6.2 touches in the opposition penalty area per 90 minutes. Those figures have risen to 5.4 and 11.8 respectively at Chelsea.

The quality of her opportunities has also improved. Her expected goals per 90 minutes have more than doubled from 0.5 to 1.1, while her shot conversion rate has increased from 10.5% to 22.2%.

It suggests Malard is benefiting from more opportunities in dangerous areas, while also making better use of the chances that come her way.

Bompastor believes the forward's improvement has been about more than just her goalscoring ability.

"She developed herself in terms of technical skills, knowledge of the game, understanding the game a little bit more, reading the game better," she says.

"She can play in different positions so we know we can use her as a nine or as a winger."

Such versatility has made Malard a valuable option for Bompastor as she chases silverware at home and abroad.

After winning the domestic treble during her first season in 2024-25, Chelsea only picked up the League Cup last season, with their third-placed finish snapping a run of six straight WSL titles.

Nine games into 2026-27, the Blues have the league's best attack and meanest defence, but a disappointing draw at home to Everton last weekend allowed champions Manchester City to overhaul them at the top of the table.

The two sides meet at Stamford Bridge on Saturday in a match live on BBC One that could be instrumental in deciding the title.

Malard will likely be leading the line, but Bompastor's ambitions for her former academy prospect are not limited to club level.

When Malard asks what Bompastor hopes she will achieve this season, the Chelsea boss sets her a clear challenge.

"I would like you to play for France next summer as the number nine and to win the World Cup," she says.

Twelve years after their first encounter, Bompastor continues to push Malard to new heights.

Mu gihe Uburundi busa n'ubutaritegura bihagije guhangana n'ingaruka zitezwe z'ibihe vya El Niño, ibimenyetso vy'ingaruka zayo vyovyo vyamaze gutangura kwibonekeza mu bice bitandukanye vy'igihugu.

Mu gace ka Nyamitanga kari muri zone Ndava ya komine Bukinanyana, intara ya Bujumbura, imvura nyinshi imaze kugwa yatumye haba inkukura zikomeye, zimaze kwonona amazu y'abanyagihugu, zongera zihungabanya uruja n'uruza kw'ibarabara rikuru Bujumbura-Cibitoke.

Uruza n'uruza ntirushoboka kuri iryo barabara. Abanyagihugu baba muri ako gace barataza basaba ko bogarukirwa, mu gihe abatwara komine Bukinanyana nta buryo ifise yo gukoresha iryo barabara.

Mariya Bukuru, umwe mu banyagihugu bo muri ako gace, avuga ko amazi y'imvura yarenze urugero agasanga abantu mu mazu yabo.

"Raba ukuntu inkukura yinjiye ngaha, ni Imana yakinze kuko ibi vyose vyava aho mw'ibarabara. Ibarabara ryari ryuzuye."

Ku birometero 33 uvuye i Bujumbura, igice c'iryo barabara caruzuyemwo amazi n'ivyondo, bigatuma uruja n'uruza rugorana. Imodoka zimwe zigerageza kurengana buhorobuhoro, mu gihe izindi zihagarara zigategereza ko amazi agabanuka.

Abanyonga imodoka bavuga ko iyo imvura iguye cane, uruja n'uruza ruhagarara burundu.

Umwe mu bashoferi ati: "Imvura iguye, nta modoka ishobora kurengana. Iyo iramutse iguye, zimwe zigarukira hariya hirya, izindi ku rya gatatu. Dusaba ko reta yadukorera iri barabara kuko ni igikoresho ca bose."

Uretse ibibazo vy'uruja n'uruza, hari n'abamaze gutakaza amazu yabo. Augustin Ntirampeba ni umwe muri bo. Inzu yiwe yarasenyutse kubera amazi y'imvura, none asigaye asaba indaro kugira aronke aho arara.

Agira ati: "Iyo imvura iguye, duca tugira ikibazo. Amazi aratera akadengera mu nzu, nta wusubira gucana, nta wusubira kurya. Tubayeho nabi cane, kuko twarabuze n'ubutabazi."

Abanyagihugu bavuga ko bamaze imyaka basaba ko iryo barabara rikorwa mu buryo burama ariko ko barindiriye amaso agahera mu nzira.

"Erega ni uko batubwira ngo baraza kurikora ariko ntibarikore. Baguma baduhenda, baraza bakayora ivu, ariko imvura iguye bigaca bigaruka kandi," ni ko umwe mu banyagihugu yavuze.

Abategetsi bo muri komine Bukinanyana bemera ko ikibazo kihari, ariko bakavuga ko ubushobozi bwa komine budahagije kugira ngo gitorerwe umuti.

Musitanteri wa komine Bukinanyana, Isaac Niyokwizera, avuga ko ibikorwa vy'ugusanura iryo barabara vyamaze kwigwa ariko ko igihe bizotangurira kitaramenyekana.

Ati: "Twebwe iyo imvura iguye, ico dukora ni ugukuraho ivyondo kugira tworohereze abanyagihugu kurengana. Ni co dushoboye kuko bisaba uburyo bwinshi kandi komine nta bushobozi bukwiye ifise."

Ibi bazo biri i Nyamitanga bifatwa nk'ikimenyetso c'ingaruka zishobora kwiyongera mu gihe ingingo zo kuzibira no gutabara zitoshirwa mu ngiro hakiri kare, na rirya hamwe hamwe ibibazo vyatanguye kwibonekeza. Hamwe ni nko kw'ibarabara Bujumbura–Rumonge, cane cane ahitwa mu Kijejeti, aho uruja n'uruza rurahungabana iyo imvura iguye. Ni ko bimeze no kw'ibarabara rihuza Gitega na Rutana.

Mu gihe abanyagihugu b'utwo duce barindiriye ko ayo mabarabara akorwa, ikibazo gisigaye ni ukumenya igihe umuti uzotorwa na cane cane ko imvura nyinshi yitezwe ishobora gutuma ingorane basanzwe bafise zirushiriza gukomera.

Izi ngorane ziri uku mu gihe reta y'Uburundi imenyesha ko ikeneye amafaranga arenga imiriyaridi 630 z'amarundi, ni ukuvuga hafi imiriyoni 210 z'amadolari y'Amerika, kugira ngo ishobore guhangana n'ingaruka za El Niño. Reta ivuga ko iza yaratanze imiliyari 10 mu bikorwa vyihutirwa biza vyaratanguye, mu gihe ayandi mafaranga yitezwe gutangwa n'abafatanyabikorwa mpuzamakungu, harimwo Ishirahamwe Mpuzamakungu ONU.

Abahinga mu bijanye n'ikirere bavuga ko El Niño ishobora gutuma hagwa imvura nyinshi hagati y'uku kwezi kwa cumi na rimwe n'ukwa kabiri kw'umwaka uza, ikongera ibiza nk'imyuzure, inkukura n'isenyuka ry'ibikorwa remezo.

The leaders of the US, Russia and China will meet late next week, according to the White House

Donald Trump, Vladimir Putin and Xi Jinping are planning to meet on the sidelines of a summit in China next week, the White House has said.

The historic meeting between the respective leaders of the US, Russia and China will take place as Trump attends the Asia-Pacific Economic Co-operation (Apec) summit in the southern city of Shenzhen, spokeswoman Olivia Wales told reporters.

"The president has made it clear that, among other topics, he will discuss the reduction of nuclear weapons in the world, whose proliferation President Trump believes is very dangerous," she said.

It is understood Iran may also be discussed during the meeting of the world's biggest nuclear powers, but not Ukraine. Russia has confirmed the meeting. China has yet to react.

No agreement was expected to follow the talks, an unnamed, senior US official said, according to news agencies AP and Reuters.

Trump will arrive in Shenzhen late on Wednesday for the two-day summit between the 21 member states. He will also take part in bilateral talks with Xi on Thursday - their fourth meeting since the US president returned to office in 2025.

"President Trump will conclude his visit to China with a trilateral meeting between the president of the United States, the president of the People's Republic of China, and the president of the Russian Federation," Wales said.

She said Trump's trip, which will also include attending an Association of South-east Asian Nations (Asean) summit in the Philippines on Tuesday, would "secure historic wins to the American people and advance America's interests in the Indo Pacific".

A nuclear weapons control treaty between the US and Russia expired in February, leaving the world's biggest nuclear arsenals without major guardrails and effectively marking an end to the arms control co-operation that helped resolve the Cold War.

The UN has urged both sides to agree a new framework without delay. Trump however said he could replace the deal with a better agreement that included China , which has been building up its arsenal.

Former senior US officials and analysts told the BBC at the time that seeking Beijing and Moscow's co-operation could create major hurdles and take years.

Xi separately hosted both Putin and Trump in Beijing just days apart earlier this year, while the US president welcomed his Chinese counterpart to Washington in September.

Beijing has become a crucial trading partner for Moscow since it launched its full-scale invasion of Ukraine in 2022, which has isolated Russia and left it subject to Western sanctions.

But a controversial US deal to import Russian diesel and the suspension of sanctions targeting the biggest buyers of Moscow's oil and gas - including China - heightened European concern about the Trump administration's softening towards the Kremlin last month.

Trump and Xi have meanwhile sought to project warmer ties at summits in Beijing and Washington this year - though little significant progress appeared to have been made on key issues such as trade, their race for AI dominance, and Taiwan.

The war in Iran has also been a sticking point, with Beijing the largest buyer of Tehran's oil and its largest trade partner.

Chinese state media reported on Friday that Xi would take part in "bilateral" talks on the sidelines of the Apec summit, citing a foreign ministry spokesman, but has not reported on the trilateral meeting.

Earlier this month, Kremlin spokesman Dmitry Peskov told Russian state media that there were "signals confirming readiness" for such talks at the summit.

Umaze kurya ifunguro rya nimugoroba, urahaze neza, ariko hashira nk'igice cy'isaha ugasanga wongeye gushaka ibyo kurya, ukajya gushakisha mu kabati kabikwamo ibiribwa. Bijya bikubaho?

Ubushakashatsi bugaragaza ko hafi kimwe cya gatatu cy'abantu barya utuntu duto (snacks) buri joro nyuma y'ifunguro rya nimugoroba. Mu rubyiruko ruri hagati y'imyaka 18 na 24, ho bane muri buri bantu batanu bananirwa kwifata ngo bareke kurya ama 'snacks'.

Inzobere mu by'imirire, Dr Kristine Beaulieu, avuga ko iki ari ikibazo gikwiye kwitabwaho. Yifashisha ubushakashatsi bugaragaza ko uko umuntu arushaho kurya mu gihe kiri munsi y'amasaha abiri mbere yo kuryama, ari ko ibyago byo kwiyongera ibiro bikabije no kugira umubyibuho ukabije birushaho kwiyongera.

Nonese kuki abantu benshi bararikira kurya mu masaha y'umugoroba? Ese ni iki wakora kugira ngo ubigabanye?

Nubwo iyo dusinziriye tumara igihe kirekire tutarya, ubushakashatsi bugaragaza ko ubushake bwo kurya bw'umuntu busanzwe bwiyongera mu masaha y'umugoroba, kabone n'iyo yaba yariye bihagije mu masaha yabanje.

Profeseri James Betts, umwarimu kuri Kaminuza ya Bath mu Bwongereza ukora ubushakashatsi ku buryo umubiri ukoresha ibiribwa n'ingufu, avuga ko imwe mu mpamvu ikomeye ibitera ari uko umusemburo witwa ghrelin, uzwi nk'utera inzara, muri rusange uba uri ku rugero rwo hejuru mu masaha y'umugoroba.

Yagize ati: "Nubwo uyu musemburo ugabanuka iyo umuntu amaze kurya, mu by'ukuri ibyo bibaho gusa nyuma yo gufata ifunguro rya mbere ry'umunsi, ariko ntibikomeze kugenda gutyo nyuma y'ifunguro rya saa sita cyangwa rya nijoro."

Ariko kandi, ibyo urya na byo bibigiramo uruhare. Amafunguro akungahaye kuri poroteyine, ibiribwa birimo 'fibre' nyinshi ndetse n'ibiribwa bituma igifu cyuzura, akenshi bituma umuntu amara igihe kinini adashonje (ahaze).

Betts avuga ko iyo umuntu atafashe ifunguro rya nimugoroba rifite intungamubiri zihagije kandi rituma ahaga, ashobora kumva umubiri ucitse intege nyuma y'igihe gito, bigatuma yongera gushaka ibyo kurya.

Hari n'abandi batinya ko bashobora kubyuka mu gicuku bashonje, bigatuma barya mbere yo kuryama. Ku bandi ho, akamenyero na ko kabigiramo uruhare.

Profeseri Suzanne Higgs, inzobere mu bijyanye n'ubushake bwo kurya (kugira appétit) wigisha kuri Kaminuza ya Birmingham mu Bwongereza, avuga ko iyo umuntu asanzwe arira ahantu hamwe, ibintu bihakikije ubwabyo bishobora gutuma yumva yongeye gushaka kurya.

Ati: "Nk'urugero, niba umuntu asanzwe arya 'snacks' igihe ari kureba televiziyo, kuyifungura gusa bishobora gutuma yumva ashaka kurya."

Amakuru ya BBC Gahuza ako kanya kuri WhatsApp yawe

Si inzara gusa yiyongera uko umunsi ugenda ushira. Ubushakashatsi bugaragaza ko muri icyo gihe abantu barushaho kugira ubushake bwo kurya ibiribwa birimo karori (calorie) nyinshi, ni ukuvuga ibitera imbaraga. Ibi biterwa n'uburyo ubwonko bwakira ibiribwa bigatuma umuntu arushaho kubyifuza, aho kuba uko umubiri uba ukeneye izindi mbaraga.

Dr Beaulieu, wigisha kuri Kaminuza ya Leeds mu Bwongereza no kuri Kaminuza ya Moncton muri Canada, avuga ko "turushaho gushaka no kwifuza ibiribwa birimo ibinure byinshi mu masaha y'umugoroba kurusha ibiribwa birimo ibinure bicye".

Yagize ati: "Uko gushaka kwishima kuvuye mu biribwa gushobora kurenga ku bimenyetso umubiri ugaragaza byerekana ko umuntu ahaze, ibyo bigatuma dushaka kongera kurya utuntu duto (snacks) cyangwa ibyo kurya biryohereye byo kwikuza [bizwi nka 'dessert'], nubwo tuba twahaze."

Ndetse n'iyo umuntu yaba yariye ifunguro rya nimugoroba rihagije, ibiribwa birimo isukari nyinshi, ibinure cyangwa umunyu bishobora gukomeza gukangura uturemangingo two mu bwonko dufitanye isano no kugira ubushake bwo kurya. Ibi bisobanura impamvu abantu benshi bumva bashaka ikindi kintu cyo kurya.

Bityo rero, niba wisanze uhagaze imbere y'akabati kabikwamo ibisuguti saa tatu z'ijoro, ntibivuze ko wabuze ubushobozi bwo kwifata cyangwa kwihangana, ahubwo hari imikorere karemano y'umubiri n'ubwonko bwawe ituma bikugora kwifata.

Nta mwanzuro uhamye uraboneka mu bushakashatsi kuri iki kibazo. Icyakora, bizwi ko kurya ifunguro ryinshi mu masaha y'ijoro bishobora gutuma igogora ry'ibiryo rigorana kandi bikabangamira uburyo busanzwe umubiri witeguramo gusinzira.

Ariko se kurya utuntu duto mbere yo kuryama byo bimeze bite? Kuri iki kibazo, ubushakashatsi ntiburagaragaza neza niba bigira ingaruka ku bitotsi.

Hari ubushakashatsi bumwe bugaragaza ko ibiribwa birimo cyane ibinyasukari bitunganyijwe hamwe n'amasukari yongerwamo mu gihe cyo kubitegura, urugero nk'umugati w'umweru, umuceri w'umweru, ibisuguti n'imitsima igezweho (cyangwa 'cake'), bishobora kuba bifitanye isano no kudasinzira neza.

Abashakashatsi batekereza ko ibyo bishobora guterwa n'uko ibyo biribwa bituma urugero rw'isukari mu maraso ruzamuka cyane hanyuma rukanagabanuka. Bishobora kandi guhindura imikorere y'imisemburo imwe n'imwe ifasha umubiri kugenzura ibitotsi n'ubushake bwo kurya.

Icyakora, kumenya neza igitera ikindi biracyagoye. Abantu badasinzira neza bashobora kuba barya cyane 'snacks' zo mu biribwa birimo isukari.

Profeseri Jonathan Johnston, inzobere mu bijyanye no gusinzira no mu isaha karemano igenzura imikorere y'umubiri, wigisha kuri Kaminuza ya Surrey mu Bwongereza, avuga ko kubura ibitotsi bihagije bitongera ubushake bwo kurya gusa, ahubwo binatuma umuntu arushaho kwifuza ibiribwa bitanga imbaraga nyinshi.

Betts avuga ko ibyo bituma bigorana kugera ku mwanzuro uhamye ku bijyanye no kumenya niba kurya utuntu duto (snacks) mu masaha y'ijoro bibangamira ibitotsi.

Yagize ati: "Nta bimenyetso bihagije biragaragaza neza uko ibintu bimeze kandi wenda ibyo bishobora kugaragaza ko abantu bamwe bashobora kutakira kimwe n'abandi ibiribwa bitandukanye barya mbere yo kuryama."

Ikintu cya mbere ni ukumenya impamvu ituma uhora ushaka kurya utuntu duto cyangwa ibiribwa byoroheje (snacks).

Higgs agira ati: "Kurya umuntu atitaye ku byo ari kurya, urugero nko kurya ari kureba televiziyo, bishobora gutuma arya byinshi kuko aba atita ku rugero amaze kurya."

Ariko Dr Beaulieu avuga ko nta mpamvu yo guhagarika burundu kurya utuntu duto mu masaha y'umugoroba.

Agira ati: "Nta cyo bitwaye kurya rimwe na rimwe, ku rugero rudakabije, ibiribwa umuntu aba yifuza cyane."

Avuga ko icy'ingenzi ari ukugira akamenyero ko guhitamo ibiribwa bifitiye umubiri akamaro.

Yongeraho ati: "Iyo ibyo biribwa umuntu ahora yifuza cyane bitaboneka mu kabati buri gihe, ariko hakabamo ibindi bifitiye umubiri akamaro, birushaho kumworohera guhitamo ibimufitiye akamaro."

Watch: US ground stop caused by issue during copper wire update, transport secretary says

An upgrade to a decades-old telecoms network in the US caused the longest nationwide grounding of flights since the 11 September 2001 attacks.

Friday's stoppage occurred when part of a key system that allows air traffic controllers and pilots to communicate was switched to fibre from copper wiring so old it has been discontinued, said US Transportation Secretary Sean Duffy on Saturday.

US planes were grounded for more than four hours, affecting thousands of flights and passengers.

Earlier Homeland Security Secretary Markwayne Mullin said there was no indication of a cyber-attack and that everybody was safe.

On Friday afternoon, a government contractor called L3Harris was continuing work on upgrading an aviation telecoms network.

As it swapped out copper lines for fibre at a remote location in the US, L3Harris installed a router - a piece of equipment which basically directs traffic across the network.

According to Duffy, that router started flooding others in the air traffic control system, sending 1,000 connection attempts every four to five seconds.

As a result, 17 out of 22 air route traffic control centres in the US experienced "instability" on voice and ground communications, said Bryan Bedford, administrator of the Federal Aviation Administration (FAA).

It took the aviation authority 45 minutes to identify where the problem was because maintenance is logged manually on paper.

This meant the FAA had to "pore through" the physical documents "to figure out who's working on what", Bedford admitted.

As a precaution as it tried to track down the cause, Bedford said the decision was made to ground all flights.

Aviation analyst Miles O'Brien described the US system as "a house that's about to be condemned".

He told the BBC: "I think most of us could look at this and go 'this is a system in the United States that we have allowed to decay'. It is worse than a fixer-upper."

Duffy said the system needed a complete overhaul, estimating a $50bn price tag.

In the meantime, he said authorities would work to determine whether it was "incompetence" or faulty equipment that led to the outage.

He also said there would be "re-evaluation" of allowing upgrades to be done during the day.

In a statement on Saturday afternoon, L3Harris confirmed it was working with the FAA to modernise the airspace communications infrastructure and said it was supporting the agency with its investigation.

"L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travelers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously," the firm said.

Juliette Kayyem, US assistant secretary of Homeland Security under President Barack Obama, questioned why an upgrade was done on one of the week's busiest days for travel.

"You don't do it on a Friday when there's lots of air traffic controllers," she said

"You try to find ways to minimise its upgrade so you're not maybe doing it across the board in a single moment but you also have to have systems that are ready to step in if the upgrade in any way begins to threaten the system," Kayyem added.

A spokesperson for L3Harris said is it "supporting the FAA in its investigation to understand the conditions that led to the 13 November ground stop of our nation's air travel".

He added: "L3Harris takes the nationwide ground stop and its impact on travellers, airlines and air traffic operations seriously."

The ground stop led to more than 8,500 delayed and nearly 8,000 cancelled flights on Friday, according to FlightAware.

The FAA's initial announcement at 15:54 EST (20:54 GMT) said all flights departing within the US would be grounded until further notice.

More than 3,500 airplanes were in the air at the time. Some were diverted to other airports and others flew on to their destinations.

Hours later, some flights were allowed to take off from San Francisco International airport.

The FAA opened skies again at 20:15 EST.

'We'll get home one day' - US travellers impacted by nationwide ground stop

All US-bound air traffic from Eurocontrol member states was suspended.

There are 42 Eurocontrol member states, including dozens of EU nations, the UK and Turkey, as well as Israel and Morocco.

Passengers travelling from the UK have been warned of possible disruption on Saturday morning.

A number of flights to the US from Heathrow airport were cancelled and delayed, but Manchester airport said no significant disruption was expected. Flights were operating as normal from Gatwick airport.

Australia's largest international airport, Sydney, had grounded all US-bound flights, but scheduled flights are now expected to depart as planned.

Air Canada also cancelled flights between the US and Canada.

Duffy said on Saturday: "We are back at full operations."

But, as he predicted on Friday, it is taking time to unwind what happened.

FlightAware said more than 5,900 flights were cancelled and more than 7,000 delayed in the US on Saturday.

Delta Air Lines and United Airlines said they were resuming operations but they both cancelled 20% of their flights on Saturday. American Airlines cancelled 520 journeys.

Meanwhile, JetBlue cancelled 40% of its scheduled journeys.

Luggage from cancelled flights at Ronald Reagan airport

In the US, UK and the EU, airlines may be liable for compensation if the reason for a delay is deemed within their control, such as a fault with the plane or pilot sickness.

As such, airlines do not have to provide compensation to passengers for air traffic control problems.

But passengers are still protected to a certain degree under US federal - and country-specific - laws.

Under the FAA Reauthorization Act of 2024, cancelled or "significantly delayed flights" - defined as three hours for domestic flights and six hours for international routes - must be offered alternative travel or a full refund of the fare if the passenger chooses not to fly.

It also requires all air carriers to issue refunds for tickets purchased with credit cards within seven business days of the request, and 20 days for tickets purchased with another form of payment. Passengers accepting a new flight cannot receive a refund.

In the US, there is no requirement for airlines to provide meal vouchers or accommodation, but some may offer complimentary support to customers.

However, if passengers are travelling from the UK to the US or flying with a UK carrier, you may have additional rights.

Under UK law, airlines have a duty to look after you when flights are delayed or cancelled for whatever reason.

a reasonable amount of food and drink (often through vouchers)

a way for you to communicate (often by refunding the cost of calls)

free accommodation, if you have to stay overnight to fly the next day

transport to and from that accommodation

If your airline is unable to arrange assistance, you have the right to organise this yourself and claim back the cost later.

The Civil Aviation Authority advises people to keep receipts and not spend more than necessary.

It was only the second such nationwide stoppage since the immediate aftermath of the al-Qaeda plane hijackings of 11 September 2001.

"This looks like the worst since 9/11, but clearly not on that scale," Dr Guy Gratton, an associate professor of aviation at Cranfield University, told BBC Verify.

Gratton pointed to a US grounding in 2023 due to a failure in the Notice to Air Missions (Notam) system.

"That lasted 1 hour and 52 minutes, delayed about 9,500 flights and cancelled about 1,300," he said.

The 2023 outage meant air traffic safety notices could no longer be published and flights were grounded until that system was restored.

GTA 6 will feature brand new protagonists Jason and Lucia - the first playable female character in any of the 3D games

After a 13-year wait, two delays, and several high-profile leaks , the launch of Grand Theft Auto 6 is fast approaching.

The next chapter in the nearly 30-year-old series, where players explore open worlds and break the law, has created an extraordinary level of anticipation.

And with developer Rockstar Games keeping their biggest release yet, tightly under wraps, even the people who helped bring the original to life aren't getting special treatment.

"We're all waiting to see what they've done," Dave Jones, GTA's co-creator, tells me, sitting alongside the original game's writer and publicist, Brian Baglow.

Have either of them been able to play the new game ahead of launch?

Baglow shakes his head. He's not complaining, though. "I've got the pre-order," he says.

Brian Baglow (left) and Dave Jones, worked on the original Grand Theft Auto

The original Grand Theft Auto was released in 1997 in Dundee, Scotland by DMA Design, a relatively small team, at least judging by later games' standards.

Following its success with puzzle game Lemmings, the studio was toying around with the idea of making a racing game, initially called Race'n'Chase.

Sitting in the state-of-the-art computer lab at Dundee's Abertay University decades on, Jones tells me the developers still felt they had to bring something new to the table.

"At DMA, we always wanted to do something different," he says. "What was the unique spin we could put on it?"

Part of the answer, he said, came in what feels like a premise gamers take for granted now - "just getting out of the car".

He says the idea of being able to not only drive but switch and steal cars, running about on foot as you did so, meant "all of a sudden you had this interesting mix of gaming coming together".

The original Grand Theft Auto came out in 1997 and featured a top-down view in 2D

After two expansion packs set in London, GTA 2 was released in 1999 and introduced rival crime syndicates

GTA 3 showed a big step up in graphics when it came out in 2001, following protagonist Claude's missions around the 3D open-world of Liberty City.

GTA Vice City, released in 2002, captured the feeling of 1980s Miami as it traced lead character's Tommy Vercetti's rise to power.

In 2004, GTA San Andreas saw players follow Carl "CJ" Johnson's story, set in the 1990s, and based in the California-inspired Los Santos

Rockstar released GTA IV in 2008 - a gritty, modern reimagining of Liberty City following Eastern European veteran Niko Bellic

In 2013, players returned to modern-day Los Santos again in GTA V, a sprawling heist thriller featuring three playable protagonists

The team envisioned a game, Jones says, where you could play as both a criminal and a police officer.

But he quickly reconsidered the second option, as it would require players to behave "by the book".

"At some point we just said, you know what, it's way more fun playing the bad guy, so that's what the game was about," he adds.

Despite some of these novel approaches to the game's design, Jones says it was a "slow burn" in sales compared with Lemmings - partly because you had to "play it to get it".

"For the whole of the year that GTA came out, it just kept going and selling and selling," says Baglow.

"And we reckoned it was the word of mouth. The people who had played it going, oh my God, have you played this game?"

Its themes of criminality and violence sparked controversy - leading to debates in the UK Parliament and calls to ban the game. Yet it later transpired much of that was generated by the game's own publisher, BMG Interactive, as a viral marketing stunt.

"We just did things that we felt were fun," says Jones. "We never at any point kind of thought, should we do that? Is it controversial? We never thought that way."

GTA 6 - all you need to know about Rockstar's blockbuster game

Although relatively basic in appearance, with its top-down 2D view and more arcade-like graphics, the original game forged the blueprint for the series' signature satire still seen in much later, more advanced GTAs today.

Despite being set in an exaggerated version of American cities, its Scottishness could still be found in its humour and its outsider perspective, says Guardian video games editor Keza MacDonald.

"It's a deeply satirical game," she says. "It really takes aim at the hyper-individualist, hyper-capitalist nature of the US."

Partly out of necessity due to their comparatively low budget and the cost of real-world licenses, the team came up with cheeky brand names and fake radio stations players could listen to while driving around and causing mayhem.

Though some of these choices were made out of limitations, Baglow says the world-building is the element he's most proud of from the original, which is still a big part of what makes a title feel like GTA.

"It's the business names, it's the radio stations, it's the lyrics, it's the DJs," he says.

"Every part of that is making you believe that this environment you're in is a big cohesive whole."

The new game's location - the fictional state of Leonida - is expected to be double the size of GTA V's map

When GTA V launched in 2013, it made $1bn (£760m) in just three days - faster than any entertainment product had achieved at the time.

The series evolved into a cultural reference point itself - something people recognised, understood and even referenced outside gaming.

"I've seen movies where someone says 'don't go all GTA on me'... it was just surreal," says Jones.

MacDonald, joining me in Glasgow's gaming cafe, RCade, tells me there's an argument now that while earlier GTAs "took a lot" from the big screen, films are now "probably more influenced by GTA" than the other way round.

She says later titles in the series have a cinematic feel, but also reflect the distinct identity it has forged for itself.

As for why Jones believes the game has become such a cultural phenomenon, he says it's the simple fact that it's "based on real life".

"It's not like a lot of games like sci-fi or adventure or fantasy," he says. "There's nothing you have to learn about it, as long as you know a city and driving."

"It means so much to so many people," says Baglow, left

GTA 6 is expected to surpass its predecessor on every level, not only in scale and scope, but also in revenue.

Already, both PlayStation and Xbox, the two platforms the game is initially releasing on, have said the game has become the most pre-ordered title in their digital stores' history.

This may be partly down to its huge size (212GB), meaning many are pre-ordering to "pre-load" the game, ready to play it immediately at launch rather than waiting to download it.

The hype has spilt into the real world, with London's Selfridges transformed into a Vice City-themed pop-up attraction and fictional GTA brands appearing on billboards across Miami, the city that inspired the game.

"Everyone is extremely excited for this," says MacDonald.

"It's hoping to be a shot in the arm for the general games industry, but also every player is looking to see what Rockstar's been doing for all this time.

"It's very rare that we have this one massive game that everybody's going to be, if not playing, then certainly interested in."

Do Jones and Baglow ever wish they were still working on the game now, given the huge amount of global attention focused on it?

"I think everybody loves having their time on it, for one, two, three versions," Jones says.

"But eventually you want to go off and do other things as well."

Baglow adds that watching "the rest of the world fall in love with the game over the last 29 years has just been joyful".

"It means so much to so many people - it's been fantastic."

A jury at Southwark Crown Court found Russell Brand guilty of one count of rape and three of sexual assault

This week, the dark side of television has come crashing into the open.

On Monday, disgraced entertainer Russell Brand was jailed for rape and sexual assault.

Twenty-four hours later, author and comedian David Walliams was unmasked and accused of preying on young women.

By Friday the Metropolitan Police had launched an investigation into further allegations about him.

Also in the last week, Married at First Sight UK has been cancelled following allegations of rape on the hit TV show.

These are all very different stories, but each can be seen as a major reckoning with abuse of power and culture in the industry.

In reality, the glut of recent days is something of a coincidence.

All these revelations began with journalistic investigations that started years ago.

From my own experience - including in my Panorama on Married at First Sight UK - I know investigations typically take a very long time to reach a conclusion, from initial tip-off, to evidence-gathering, corroboration, getting responses, and eventually reporting.

"The truth is, these stories have a long build up. It can be incredibly difficult to get [them] in the papers," Sunday Times columnist Hadley Freeman told me.

In the case of Brand, there was then a police investigation too, before an outcome was reached in court.

Together these stories represent the consequences of changes that began years ago, rather than a sudden cultural shift in the entertainment industry.

It should also be said that Walliams denies the allegations against him . The men accused of rape and sexual misconduct on MAFS UK have also denied all the allegations.

What has changed is that women (because it almost always is women) have seen others speaking up - which, according to broadcaster Kirsty Wark, has given them "courage to do the same". She describes those who have come forward as "beyond brave".

When looking at what’s driving more women to speak up, much can be traced back to the revelations about Harvey Weinstein and the #MeToo movement.

It changed the perception of whether victims would be believed.

In the past, women alleging this sort of behaviour faced barriers - being seen as opportunistic, fearing retaliation, believing they might be the only one.

Now, there can be a snowball effect. Once one, two or three come forward, that prompts others to revisit their experiences - which they may have dismissed or subdued.

"There is more of a sense that you will now be listened to," said Freeman.

It's also clear that when women see action taken, it can encourage others to speak up as well - as it helps counter the widely-held assumption that reporting abuse results in nothing.

Married at First Sight UK cancelled after rape allegations

When another high-profile man, MasterChef presenter Gregg Wallace, faced accusations of a very different and much lesser order, relating mostly to inappropriate sexual language and humour, the reaction was similar.

Last summer, an independent inquiry upheld dozens of claims against him, and he was sacked . Wallace said "none of the serious allegations" against him had been upheld but that he was "deeply sorry for any distress caused".

One young woman I spoke to in my investigation into Wallace texted me at the time, to give her reaction to his sacking.

"I really believe this will encourage young girls going into the TV industry to have the courage to speak up, if they feel something is wrong," she told me.

But unions say it is still difficult for junior freelance workers, who often find their income unstable and unpredictable, to speak up.

Vulnerable workers "continue to fear raising concerns", said head of broadcast union Bectu, Philippa Childs.

She's echoed by Freeman, who said an "attitude of protecting the talent" remained.

"There will always be wealthy famous predators," she said. But, she added: "Hopefully more and more people at TV stations and movie studios are willing to hear these young people and will take them seriously”.

For more senior people in TV, raising the alarm can also be difficult.

Earlier this week, comedian Lucy Beaumont told Sky News: "The reason high-profile people are not saying anything is because they lose work, because you're seen that you might be a trouble causer. It does need to be said that there needs to be some intervention."

Panorama investigates allegations that raise serious concerns that welfare procedures on Married at First Sight UK have failed contributors, leaving them at risk of harm.

Social media has also played a role in encouraging people to speak up.

And policing investigations have had to keep pace - and adapt - with media scrutiny often prompting authorities to investigate.

Attitudes towards women who speak up are also starting to change – although not always.

Some of what unfolded in court during the Russell Brand case felt like a throwback to how rape cases used to be conducted.

Many have commented on Brand's lawyer's defence tactics against the accusers on the stand - behaviour Freeman said would have been "standard" in the past.

But Freeman noted it was heartening to hear the judge’s remarks in summing up the case - which have also been widely shared by women online and praised for dispelling rape myths.

When Mr Justice Bennathan sentenced Brand to ten-and-a-half years, he told him: "Whatever women wear, wherever they go, indeed whatever they drink, they retain the right to say no."

"I think attitudes have changed,” said Freeman. “It doesn't mean those assaults don't happen any more but attitudes around them have changed.”

Events of the past few weeks highlight how figures who rose to prominence in the nineties and noughties did so in an era with different standards.

Lad culture and celebrity status shielded Brand and others from scrutiny .

Now, behaviour once dismissed as eccentricity or womanising is increasingly being reassessed and called out. Times are catching up with some men of that era.

However, it would be an error to assume this sort of behaviour is confined to the past.

"This is not just about nineties/noughties culture," Wark told me. "It can't be dismissed as a hangover of the past, this is about right now and the industry changes that must happen.

"There will be more cases to come, sexual abuse, coercive control, verbal and physical abuse. It is not OK, and it never was OK."

David Walliams lost a legal bid to stop the claims against him being made public

This week, comedian Deborah Frances-White told BBC Radio 4's The World at One that young women were "definitely" still being exploited in the comedy industry.

And in the past few days, I've had tip-offs about other celebrities allegedly abusing their power. No doubt other journalists have too.

None of those is reportable, yet. As Freeman said: "There are other names out there, but you and I couldn't name them as we'd be sued".

But one "cheering thing", she said, was that the sort of jokes and innuendos from the nineties and noughties, or even the optics of seeing a much older man with a younger girl would no longer be "glossed over".

"It wouldn't be laughed at, and it wouldn't be 'nudge nudge'," Freeman said. "That kind of open, in your face, weirdness won't happen any more".

"On the downside, that may make it harder to identify predators, if it means these things are kept more in the shadows."

Channel 4's office in central London. Its bosses will be questioned by MPs next week following the cancellation of Married at First Sight UK

Then there’s the use of gagging orders and other legal routes often used by celebrities and media organisations to stop women speaking out.

Last week, a High Court judge rejected an injunction request by Walliams, clearing the way for him to be named.

"There are lots of barriers to speaking out, and those that have access to wealth or fame will often use legal measures to deter alleged victims from doing so," Harriet Wistrich, from the Centre for Women's Justice, told me.

This week, multiple government ministers have spoken against non-disclosure agreements and called for further restrictions on their use.

Next week, Culture Secretary Lisa Nandy will convene industry leaders to urge them to improve safeguarding practices - while Channel 4 bosses are due to appear in front an MPs on Tuesday.

When MAFS UK was cancelled, Channel 4 said the programme had "run its course" and apologised to the women involved in the investigation.

It said the review found that in Channel 4 and production company CPL's handling of the issues raised at the time, there was no breach of Ofcom's broadcasting code.

There is growing recognition that those at the top of media organisations have a responsibility to root out abuse. It can't just be down to the victims.

"People in positions of power have a duty to speak up too," said Wark.

"Broadcasters, production companies and those financing productions all have a responsibility to ensure protections are upheld," added Josephine Brassey, from Women in Film and TV, while Philippa Childs urged the creative industries to accept that their current internal reporting mechanisms were "inadequate".

What everyone seems to agree on is that this can't be another empty tipping point with no real, lasting change.

Maybe this time it could really be a watershed moment.

Spread by midges, bluetongue poses no threat to the public or food safety

The first case of Bluetongue in Northern Ireland this season has been confirmed on a farm in Kilkeel, County Down.

Officials from the Department of Agriculture, Environment and Rural Affairs (Daera) said the virus had been detected in three sheep.

There will be no additional movement restrictions or disease control zones, because the virus has been present in Northern Ireland since November 2025.

The minister, Andrew Muir, said the discovery of the virus was "disappointing but not unexpected", given the spread of the disease in Great Britain and Ireland.

The Chief Veterinary Officer, Brian Dooher, urged local farmers to be alert to any symptoms in their livestock.

The confirmation of the virus in Kilkeel comes after more than 100 cases across the Republic of Ireland in recent months.

Cases in England have been increasing, with 2,950 now confirmed.

There have been 512 cases in Wales and 57 in Scotland.

The mild winter means more of the biting midge that spreads the disease are likely to have survived and become infectious this season.

Muir said awareness was key, adding: "Continued vigilance and strict biosecurity measures remain of paramount importance and I would once again urge all farmers to report any suspicion of disease to Daera.

"It is important that I reiterate that Bluetongue poses no threat to public health nor to food safety – milk and meat are safe to consume."

Dooher said any suspected cases on farms should be reported to Daera.

"Active surveillance is ongoing at abattoirs alongside post-import testing of susceptible animals imported from mainland EU countries.

"I also want to stress the importance of safe and responsible sourcing of animals."

The disease was first detected in Northern Ireland near Bangor in County Down in November 2025.

A number of other herds along the eastern coast of Northern Ireland have also been affected.

Farmers have been urged to vaccinate their animals.

The disease affects ruminants such as cattle, sheep, goats and deer.

Jojo the gorilla has spent his life alone. Can he finally find a companion?

In 2015, a young male gorilla named Jojo took his first tentative steps onto grass.

Until that moment, the 11-year-old ape had spent almost his entire life in a tiny cage at a private zoo in Gabon, after being taken from the wild as an infant. His family had been killed by the poachers who took him.

More than a decade later, Jojo is settled into a sanctuary – but he still lives alone. He hasn't had a family since he was taken, or indeed any gorilla friends.

Jojo's carers at the Lekedi Foundation in Gabon want to find a companion - possibly another rescued or zoo-bred gorilla – that Jojo could live and bond with. But finding him a friend - and bringing them into his life - is not straightforward.

"He's probably the most extreme case of isolation I've ever seen in a great ape," says Prof Gillian Forrester from the University of Sussex, who is studying Jojo as part of research into great ape psychology and how to help rescued animals recover from trauma.

Jojo's keeper Maxe Anaclet Makaba: 'He definitely feels lonely - you can see it in his eyes'

Jojo was less than a year old – an infant clinging to his mother – when he was captured and sold.

Most gorillas spend the first 14 to 19 years of their life in an embedded family unit but he was kept completely alone and on public display at the private zoo that bought him.

Maxe Anaclet Makaba, who is head keeper at Lekedi and sees Jojo nearly every day, says it is clear he "craves human interaction".

"He will even go to the trouble of gathering leaves for us to hold, so that we [trade them] for a treat – to interact with us," he says.

Jojo also calls out when women he knows well visit his enclosure and then leave, making sounds that silverback males use to summon the females in the wild, explains Éric Willaume, who runs the sanctuary.

When Jojo first arrived at the sanctuary after spending years in a small iron cage, he didn't look directly at people

Jojo is one of the more than 6,000 African primates estimated to have been bought or sold in the global trade of apes and other primates between 2000 and 2023. Thousands more are trafficked illegally for use as exotic pets, wild meat, and traditional medicine, the Pan African Sanctuary Alliance says. , external

Experts believe when baby great apes are taken from their group at a young age like Jojo, they are left traumatised.

"If they're old enough to understand what happened to them, to understand their family was killed, they just lose the will to live," explains conservationist Tony King, from UK charity the Aspinall Foundation. "You see it in their eyes – the light goes out. I never knew where that expression came from, but I've seen it in gorillas."

King – who specialises in rehabilitating rescued great apes – remembers rescuing two infant sister gorillas who were brought to a sanctuary in the Congo Basin.

"They were clinging to each other," he says. "They stayed together in a little tight ball for about three days before they sort of unravelled. I think that's what kept them alive."

Sisters Likendze and Matoko clutch each other after they were brought in a wooden crate to the Project Protection des Gorilles sanctuary in the Congo

African charity the Gorilla Rehabilitation and Conservation Education (Grace) Center uses what it calls "gorilla-led" rehabilitation. When the team rescues a young gorilla from the pet trade, they put it with a group as soon as possible so they can socialise and essentially learn to be a gorilla.

But Jojo's case is unusual. He is fully mature and showing signs of harmful, chronic stress, according to Forrester.

In a game-changing approach to studying anxiety and trauma in apes, she has used a thermal camera to film Jojo's face. This allows her to monitor blood flow, revealing what appears to be a chronically cold nose.

It's a sign of a malfunctioning stress response. When any primate – a human, chimp or gorilla - is stressed, blood flow to the eyes and ears increases. It puts them on high alert for danger, but leaves their nose, temporarily, colder. For Jojo, this "nasal dip" as it is known, does not seem to recover.

"Being connected to others is incredibly important to our psychology as great apes," Forrester says. "Having another individual to share his life with would be so healing for him.

"I would assume other gorillas would help him process this grief and trauma."

Thermal imaging of Jojo's face reveals signs of chronic stress, with a persistently cold nose indicating a potentially disrupted stress response

Dr Katie Fawcett, from the Grace Center, says it's also "essential" for an animal to form social relationships to be considered for release into the wild - which is the ultimate goal for Jojo's keepers.

The bonds between gorillas – what we would call friendship - is key to their society, adds Dr Robin Morrison from the University of Zurich, who studies the social lives of mountain gorillas. In one recent study, she discovered that female mountain gorillas would seek out females they knew, even if they hadn't seen them for many years, when joining a group.

And she says a big part of a gorilla's normal social life is "just sitting together quietly sharing space".

But Jojo has never been given the opportunity to sit quietly with another gorilla.

No one knows how Jojo will react to a companion. Moving an animal from an accredited zoo would be a decision for an international committee and based on genetics, health and the animals' personalities and compatibility.

Any introduction to another animal would be done very carefully – perhaps giving them an object that smells of the other before they see each other.

These slow, cautious ape introductions do happen – when an animal moves from one zoo group to another, for example. Forrester has contacted a number of accredited zoos to explore the possibility of doing this for Jojo. But those discussions have fizzled out with no sign of progress.

The problem, she says, is "there aren't clear processes in place to do these kinds of trans-locations".

Encounters between two or more separate gorilla groups are complex social events

The international rules and processes for moving captive gorillas across international borders - from one zoo or safari park to another - are designed for breeding programmes.

"They're not designed for reintroductions into the wild, or to find companions for animals that might need them," says Forrester.

And because Jojo, who is probably in his 20s, has reached maturity, King thinks it might be too late for him to bond with other gorillas.

"Jojo's situation is unique, but he is probably best where he is," King says, adding that introducing him to another animal could, somewhat ironically, be a source of more stress for him.

Prof Forrester studies Jojo as part of research to understand how our understanding of human mental health - particularly stress and trauma - can be applied to our great ape relatives

Being alone is also natural, even relatively common, for mature male gorillas. According to Morrison, about a third of adult males are solitary. "When they reach adolescence, they tend to disperse and spend a good chunk of their life on their own."

Solo males will try to persuade females to form a group with them, but some don't succeed and may feel lonely as a consequence, Morrison believes. "If we think of loneliness in an evolutionary context - this mismatch between the social interactions they want and the social interactions they're getting. I suspect feeling lonely is part of the natural, evolutionary drive to attract females."

But while those phases – of family life and adult solitude - play a role in wild gorilla society, Jojo was forced into solitary confinement as an infant.

Morrison believes Jojo is probably both traumatised and lonely.

"[In the wild] gorillas move together, find food together, sleep together," she says. "So much of their lives is just being with this group."

That is what Jojo's keepers, Forrester, and others want for Jojo. A friend. Maybe a female, or a compatible male.

"It would be good for him to have a companion," says keeper Makaba. "Because being alone is like being cut off from the world - it's like being in prison.

"Having another gorilla there would be a good thing for him."

Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba has signalled his intention to run for president in the next elections

In Uganda's military, even senior generals are finding that their rank offers little protection from the wrath of the country's powerful army chief.

Over the past 15 months, at least a dozen generals and senior officers have been arrested under Gen Muhoozi Kainerugaba, who is also the son of President Yoweri Museveni, in a crackdown that has unsettled the military's top ranks.

The arrests come amid growing political tensions over who will succeed Museveni, who has ruled Uganda for four decades.

Gen Kainerugaba, 52, is widely seen as a potential successor, although his ambitions appear to be facing resistance within the ruling party.

This week, he threatened Vice-President Jessica Alupo with dismissal and possible arrest, while suggesting he should take her position.

The ruling National Resistance Movement (NRM) has, however, rejected reports that its senior leadership had rejected a proposal to back Gen Kainerugaba as the next president, describing the claims as "completely false".

This has all fuelled speculation that the arrests are part of an effort to sideline military officers opposed to the general's presidential ambitions.

Others see the arrests as evidence of an anti-corruption drive in which senior commanders are held to account.

At the centre of the tension are two powerful powerful institutions: the military, where Gen Kainerugaba wields considerable influence, and the NRM, where questions about his political ambitions appear to be dividing senior figures.

A recent meeting of NRM's top leadership ended without agreement on a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Museveni's successor, according to the AFP news agency.

Five party sources who attended the closed-door meeting told AFP that a vote was abandoned after several members spoke against the proposal.

Uganda's news website ChimpReports, however, said that most members who spoke backed the general's potential presidency, although some questioned his readiness for civilian leadership.

In a statement on Thursday, NRM Secretary General Richard Todwong Awany confirmed that the party had met on 10 November to discuss "political, social and economic issues".

He dismissed reports that the meeting had rejected a proposal to position Gen Kainerugaba as Uganda's next president, saying the party would communicate any decisions "through the right channel, at the right time".

President Yoweri Museveni's grandson (standing up, shaking the president's hand) has joined the army, alongside his father (sitting down, wearing camouflage)

Dr Gerald Bareebe, a Ugandan-born political scientist at Canada's York University, sees a connection between the arrests and political manoeuvring over Museveni's succession, often referred to as the "Muhoozi Project".

"Senior officers believed not to support the project have been arrested, detained or charged with corruption and treason," he tells the BBC.

He says the allegations against some officers were widely viewed as politically motivated, reflecting growing divisions within the military over the succession question.

Some of those detained have since been released, apparently after securing the general's forgiveness.

The detention of one of the country's most prominent former commanders, Lt Gen Peter Elwelu , has brought the crackdown into sharper focus.

The former deputy army chief was detained on 2 November over allegations that he had plotted to destabilise the eastern Teso region.

His fall from grace followed a series of social media posts by Kainerugaba, who accused him of treachery and announced that he had been stripped of his three-star rank and demoted.

"The traitor Peter Elwelu is hereby stripped of his ranks. He is demoted to Private," Kainerugaba wrote on X.

He also claimed that more than 20 soldiers linked to Elwelu had been arrested.

The announcement raised legal questions, with Ugandan media reporting that military regulations do not allow a senior officer to be stripped of his rank through a social media post.

The army later confirmed Elwelu's detention, saying they had recovered 15 guns, military uniforms and two pickup trucks linked to him. His family has rejected the allegations.

Elwelu is among at least a dozen generals and senior officers detained since April 2025, according to an investigation by Uganda's Daily Monitor newspaper.

They include three former military intelligence chiefs who once oversaw some of Uganda's most sensitive security operations.

Maj Gen James Birungi, a former head of defence intelligence and security, was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption.

He was charged before a military court but later released after Gen Kainerugaba announced that he had "forgiven" him.

Another former intelligence chief, Maj Gen Abel Kandiho, was detained in September this year over allegations of providing false intelligence and treachery. He remains in detention, according to the Daily Monitor.

His predecessor, Brig-Gen Charles Bakahumura, was also arrested in September over similar allegations, but was later released after the army chief announced that he had forgiven him.

Other officers have faced accusations ranging from stealing military fuel to taking money to spy on military communications.

The military has defended the arrests as part of efforts to tackle corruption and criminality within the armed forces.

Maj Gen James Birungi was arrested in August 2025, on allegations including treason, terrorism and corruption

Ugandan security analyst Freddie David Egesa says the arrests reflect investigations involving different security agencies, rather than an army-led purge.

He argues that detaining senior officers helps protect witnesses and demonstrates the seriousness of the anti-corruption drive.

"Gen Muhoozi has the overall duty to permit the investigation team to arrest these high-profile people, in consultation with the commander-in-chief," Egesa says, adding: "The arrests are not summarily done."

But Bareebe sees a wider political motive, arguing that officers suspected of opposing to Gen Kainerugaba's presidential ambitions are being targeted.

"The result is a broad purge that has affected both serving and retired officers perceived to be anti-Muhoozi," he says.

He points to divisions between the elite Special Forces Command (SFC), which he says is largely loyal to the president's son, and army commanders who remain unconvinced about his succession.

The allegations against the officers are at different stages, with some facing charges, others in detention without publicly announced charges, and several having been released.

Bareebe also questions whether military trials can deliver independent proceedings.

"Many Ugandans regard the charges as politically motivated and therefore expect little justice," he adds.

He alleges that some officers have had charges dropped after closed-door negotiations with the president and his son, during which they were pressured to declare support for Gen Kainerugaba.

Government spokesperson Allan Kasujja dismissed the claims of a succession fallout as "hogwash".

Unlike his predecessors, who communicated through official military channels, Gen Kainerugaba frequently uses X to announce arrests, criticise public officials and comment on domestic and international affairs. Some have sparked diplomatic controversy.

On the night of 9 November, he turned his attention to Vice-President Jessica Alupo, demanding to take her job.

"Whoever is in that office should prepare to hand it over soon," he wrote, in posts that he later deleted.

He also questioned Alupo's loyalty and threatened her dismissal, adding that the government would operate "on military terms", if he became his father's deputy.

The following day, his X account, which had nearly 1.4 million followers, became inaccessible.

It was unclear whether he deactivated it himself, which he has done before, or the platform had suspended it.

Alupo remains in office and has yet to respond publicly.

Vice-President Jessica Alupo is yet to respond to Gen Kainerugaba's posts questioning her loyalty

Egesa says Gen Kainerugaba's controversial posts reflect his preferred style of communicating, but adds that security analysts are assessing their implications for Uganda's political and military stability.

Bareebe, however, sees them as part of a broader effort by the army chief to extend his influence into civilian politics.

He says the public confrontation with senior political figures illustrates how the succession debate was spilling beyond the army and into the ruling party.

Gen Kainerugaba was appointed army chief in March 2024, after previously commanding the SFC, which is responsible for protecting the president and strategic installations.

Under Uganda's military structure, he reports directly to Museveni, giving him considerable influence over the army.

Bareebe argues that the SFC's loyalty to the president and his son could prove crucial in any future transfer of power.

"The regular army remains important but has been sidelined by the SFC, which now functions as a personal army for Museveni and his son," he adds.

At the heart of the tension is the question of who will succeed Museveni, 82, who has ruled Uganda since 1986, when his rebel National Resistance Army seized power after a five-year guerrilla war.

He was sworn in for a seventh elected presidential term earlier this year , extending his rule into a fifth decade.

Gen Kainerugaba has been regarded as a possible successor and has indicated that he intends to seek the presidency in 2031, when his father's current term is due to end.

He also leads the Patriotic League of Uganda, a political movement that has mobilised support around his leadership.

But recent developments suggest that a transfer of power from father to son may be more complicated than his supporters anticipated.

At the recent meeting of the NRM leadership, one official reportedly urged Museveni to retire his son from the military and give him a civilian role to gain administrative experience, AFP reported.

Local media reported that some party officials consider Gen Salim Saleh, Museveni's younger brother, better suited for civilian leadership.

There is, however, no indication that he is interested in becoming president.

Others reportedly defended Gen Kainerugaba, pointing to his military leadership, anti-corruption campaign and grassroots political mobilisation.

Bareebe says opposition to the proposed succession has grown within the NRM, with both veteran figures and younger members concerned about what they see as an attempt to secure power through coercion.

He suggests Museveni's reluctance to move his son out of the military could reflect the importance of retaining control of the army during any transition.

"The underlying calculation appears to be that, so long as Muhoozi controls the SFC, he can use it to capture power even in an event of a contested transition," he says.

The military has been central to Museveni's hold on power, making the loyalties of senior commanders particularly important as succession questions intensify.

The family's military influence has also drawn attention to the possibility of a political dynasty spanning generations, with Gen Kainerugaba's son, Ruhamya, recently graduating from Britain's Sandhurst military academy.

The succession debate is unfolding against a backdrop of sustained pressure on the opposition.

Veteran opposition politician Kizza Besigye remains in detention on treason charges, which he denies.

Bobi Wine, who came second to Museveni in this year's presidential election, has gone into exile in the US, after being threatened by Gen Kainerugaba .

The government has consistently defended its security operations as lawful and necessary to maintain stability.

But the arrests, his son's threats and competing accounts of divisions within the ruling party have intensified questions about how Uganda's next political transition might unfold, and what role his family may play.
